result.key_differentiator: Plan A answers the question posed — whether adopters reduce DraftKings spend — while Plan B has drifted into a causal-mechanism study of wallet substitution effects that requires different data, assumptions, and evidentiary standards than the fund can sustain.
result.rationale: The research question is narrow and concrete: Do customers who start trading on Kalshi subsequently reduce their spend and activity on DraftKings? This is a single-name positioning question for a concentrated fundamental fund, not a broad market-effect study. Plan A recognizes this and designs for it. Plan A directly estimates whether Kalshi adopters reduce DraftKings deposits, retention, and transaction counts using a cohort event-study design with matching. It produces a defensible counterfactual — the adopters' own pre-adoption trajectory — and tests whether the post-period deviates from it. Success is concrete and judgeable: you see an event-time path, you precommit your kill criterion, you know whether you got a signal or noise. The validation is appropriate to the scope — placebos test specificity (is this really about event contracts or just a user-churn effect?), pre-trends establish the counterfactual is parallel, matching covariates report whether the treatment and control groups are comparable. This is a plan designed for a PM who will ask "what would have to be true for it to be wrong" — the answer is "pre-trends would have to be non-parallel, placebos would have to show the same drop, the effect would have to match the MDE floor." The plan matches the firm: they buy transaction panels routinely, have done cohort analyses, and do not need tick data or ML. The output — position-sized changes on DraftKings — is the exact kind of thing they use. Because this is a concentrated fund with explicit downside to being wrong on a named position, Type I error dominates: a false positive on DraftKings cannibalization that changes position size costs real money with no diversification hedge. Plan A's demanding standard — matching, balanced panel, pre-trend tests, placebos, wild bootstrap — is appropriate to this error structure. Plan A sequences for information: build the matching and validate on pre-period data first, then run the main event-study design, then run placebos and robustness. You can kill the idea early if pre-trends are non-parallel or coverage is poor. Plan B has drifted into a different, broader question. It asks whether within-user changes in Kalshi share mechanically predict changes in DraftKings deposits beyond the mechanical amount, controlling for total wallet. This is a question about the elasticity of substitution, about whether Kalshi cannibalization is stronger than category substitution, about whether the effect is concentrated in high-tenure users. These are important questions for market-sizing or for understanding how the gaming ecosystem might reorder itself, but they are not the question asked. The fund does not need to know whether the effect is "brand switching" (H2) or "category substitution" (H3) or concentrated in long-tenured users (H4). They need to know whether Kalshi adoption predicts lower DraftKings spend on the names they hold. By widening the scope to wallet-level mechanism tests, Plan B has created a much harder evidentiary problem. It introduces causal mechanisms that cannot be observed (whether a within-user share rise is exogenous or endogenous to total-wallet changes), requires stronger assumptions (the Arellano-Bond lag structure, the IV strategy using "affinity × national volume"), and produces a quantity — an elasticity or a mechanically-adjusted causal effect — that is harder to defend to a PM than "here is the event-time path, here are pre-trends, here are placebos." Plan B's error structure is also mismatched. It designs for Type II error — broadening the design to reduce false negatives, running multiple specifications, cross-checking event studies with regression discontinuities, using permutation and randomization inference. This makes sense if you are trying to establish a generalizable market effect and want to avoid gating out a real phenomenon. But for a concentrated fund making position-sizing calls on named companies, Type I error is the expensive error. A false positive on DraftKings cannibalization that is driven by an un-adjusted confound costs money; missing a real but smaller effect is a missed profit but does not require the position to be sized down. Plan B's design is expensive in human and computational resources — it requires IV validation, wild bootstraps, careful attribution for late-entry structural breaks (the 2025 DK/FD sports-contract regime), balance-testing under different attrition scenarios, out-of-sample prediction on 2025 cohorts. For a three-person data team, this is overspecification. It also does not sequence for information: the IV strategy is front-loaded even though it is a second-order concern (only matters if you want to isolate the causal mechanism within the treatment group), and the pre-trends test is rolled in with other validation rather than leading. Most importantly, Plan B has introduced a structural break (sportsbooks' own prediction markets) as a late-stage complication. Plan A's matching can accommodate this because it is cohort-based; Plan B's regression approach requires a regime shift. Plan B flags it in pitfalls but does not resolve it cleanly — it says to estimate the 2025 regime separately, but the whole point of adopting Kalshi in 2025 is different if DraftKings itself now offers event contracts. Plan A sidesteps this by restricting to pre-structural-break cohorts or flagging the post-break regime separately, which is cleaner. Plan A is also clearer about what it cannot measure: "Dollars observed, not trades: sports-specific substitution is inference, not measurement." This is the right epistemic stance. Plan B claims it will measure mechanism (substitution vs expansion vs switching) when mechanism is inherently unobserved — you can see dollar flows but not the intent behind them. For a single-name question with asymmetric error costs and a concentrated fund, Plan A is the right design. It is simpler, faster to execute, produces a result that is judgeable and defensible, and matches the firm's infrastructure and risk tolerance. Plan B is a better design for a question the fund is not asking.
issues_with_winner: The plan restricts to users with ≥$50 pre-adoption DraftKings spend, which excludes potential switchers who were low-intensity at baseline — if the most material cannibalization is among new-to-DraftKings users who adopt Kalshi instead, the plan misses it (though the pipeline does count adopters without pre-period activity separately).

Payouts are excluded from the outcome but included in net-dollar measures as robustness; if Kalshi adoption changes payout frequency (lower on both, or retained longer), the story can flip between gross and net — the plan flags this but does not pre-commit to which is headline.

The matching uses OLS slope in −6..−1 as a propensity covariate, which can amplify pre-trend heterogeneity if some users were already in secular decline; the exclusion of users down >50% in −3..−1 vs −6..−4 in robustness helps, but this is buried.
issues_with_loser: The plan conflates the research question with a mechanism study: the fund asked whether Kalshi adopters reduce DraftKings spend, not why, and the plan spends most of its effort isolating within-user wallet elasticity, brand switching, and concentration by tenure, none of which the fund asked about.

The IV strategy (affinity × national non-sports Kalshi volume) is theoretically unmotivated for this context: why would a user's pre-period affinity for non-sports Kalshi combined with national sports-contract volume be a valid instrument for within-user share changes? The exclusion restriction is opaque and difficult for the fund to defend.

The plan introduces sportsbooks' own prediction markets as a structural break mid-analysis, requiring regime-splitting and out-of-sample validation on 2025 cohorts, which complicates the design and introduces look-ahead bias (2025 is not yet complete at the time of writing).

The denominator problem (the regressor Kalshi share contains DraftKings in the denominator) is real and the plan correctly flags it, but the solution — testing against a permuted null — is a workaround, not a solution. The fundamental issue is that the estimand is ambiguous: is the plan trying to measure the effect of exogenous Kalshi adoption on DK spending, or the elasticity of DK spending with respect to share? These are different and require different controls.

By widening to wallet-level substitution, the plan requires much stronger assumptions about balance, common causes, and unconfoundedness. A state × month effect and an instrument can only go so far when you are trying to separate selection bias (who adopts Kalshi?) from true substitution.

The Callaway–Sant'Anna event study is a robustness check, but the plan says it is credible only if the β × mean Δshare matches the ATT within ~2×. This is a weak agreement criterion and could mask specification-dependent results.

The plan is resource-intensive for a three-person data team: Arellano–Bond, wild bootstrap, permutation tests, IV validation, 2025 out-of-sample prediction, and balancing tests across tenure and decile cuts is a large workload and risks not finishing in a useful timeframe.

result.key_differentiator: Plan A matches the actual research question and this firm's constraints; Plan B answers a different, broader question that requires infrastructure and causal claims this firm cannot sustain.
result.rationale:
This is a question about a specific named company (DraftKings) and a specific economic phenomenon (cannibalization from a named competitor), asked by a fundamental long/short fund that needs to change position sizing on identified securities. That signature matches Plan A's framing throughout.

Goal-mismatch is decisive here. Plan B is designed to estimate a population treatment effect—answering 'does Kalshi adoption reduce spending on DraftKings in general?' across a cohort. It produces a causal claim (ATT) with confidence bands, optimized for breadth and generalizability. Plan A is designed to measure the relationship between market shares and behavior in a specific user base, with explicit heterogeneity by tenure and pre-period spend, and asks what would have to be true for the effect to be wrong—exactly what a PM needs before sizing a position.

Firm fit reinforces this. The fund has three-person data team, buys transaction panels, does not have ML infrastructure, and needs output defensible to a PM asking 'what falsifies this?' Plan A delivers exactly that: permutation nulls, placebo tests, pre-trends, wallet accounting, and event-study cross-checks, all using methods (panel regression, matching on observables) this firm can understand and inspect. Plan B uses cohort-level design with propensity-score matching, wild cluster bootstrap over cohorts, partial identification bounds, and inverse-probability weighting—more methodologically sophisticated but less inspectable to a fundamental shop. Plan A's output is also a dollar figure per 10-point share shift, directly usable for position sizing. Plan B's output is average post-period deposit dollars under treatment, which does not immediately translate to position conviction without additional inference.

Error asymmetry strongly favors Plan A. A concentrated long/short book with a named short position on DraftKings has asymmetric downside: being wrong about cannibalization can mean a large loss, not a diversified miss. This makes Type I error (false positive for substitution) much more costly than Type II (missing a real effect). Plan A is designed for this: it leads with a permutation null that the analyst must beat at the 5th percentile, uses Driscoll–Kraay robustness and Arellano–Bond lags (not standard for this question but appropriate for ruling out spurious dynamics), validates against placebo outcomes (grocery, streaming, general merchandise) and non-legal-state error floors, and pre-commits kill criteria. Plan B minimizes Type II risk—using 80% power, 1:5 matching, and partial identification to avoid discarding real effects—which is the opposite of what this error structure demands.

Evidence standard is matched correctly in Plan A. The firm cannot produce a causal estimate that would survive a journal's standards, and Plan A does not try—it answers a more limited question: conditional on the data, does this user's substitution behavior look mechanical or behavioral, and is it concentrated in tenure/spend groups that matter? The permutation null answers this. Plan B promises a causal claim (ATT, confidence intervals) that in truth rests on the assumption that matching on observables is sufficient, which this firm's PM will not believe without a randomized experiment. Plan A punts the causal claim and instead delivers the raw correlation and a validation that it is not purely mechanical, which is defensible.

Sequencing and parsimony favor Plan A. The simplest question is: does the raw correlation between Kalshi share rise and DK deposit decline hold within users, and survive the mechanical null? Plan A answers that first, before any matching or propensity scoring. Plan B makes matching and cohort definition the gatekeeper—if matching fails (dropped adopters, low F-stat, high SMD), the entire design breaks. Plan A's permutation null can succeed or fail independently of any modeling choice.

Plan A also has adaptive sequencing: it says what happens if the permutation fails (the event study becomes the lead), if the pre-trends fail (selection bounds), if whales dominate (report separately), if attrition is unbalanced (Lee bound). Plan B lists the contingencies in Pitfalls but does not adapt the analysis—it still runs the same specification under all scenarios.

Inspectability for AI execution is stronger in Plan A. Plan A produces: hand-audited descriptor dictionary with drift audit (inspectable), wallet accounting (summing to 100%, inspectable), event-study plots with matched strata (inspectable), permutation distribution (inspectable), placebo coefficients (inspectable). Plan B produces: matched cohort weights, SMD table, event-time coefficients by cohort. Both are inspectable, but Plan A's intermediate outputs (taxonomy audit, wallet accounting) catch data quality issues earlier.

Plan A is not perfect. The methodology is dense (Driscoll–Kraay, leave-out share, affinity IV, Callaway–Sant'Anna, randomization inference) and may be overkill for a panel of a few thousand users. The permutation null, while appropriate, requires careful implementation and a PM may not immediately trust it. The IV strategy (national non-sports Kalshi volume × affinity to predict individual adoption) is somewhat contrived and the relevance condition (F > 20) is not guaranteed. The analyst will need to learn some new tools.

Plan B's strengths are real but misaligned with the goal. It is more carefully sequenced within its own logic (matching first, then event-time estimation), the event-study design is cleaner conceptually, and it is more likely to be published or defended in a statistical seminar. It is the right plan for answering 'on average, do Kalshi adopters spend less on DraftKings?' But that is not the question asked. The question is whether DraftKings is being cannibalized by Kalshi in a way that changes the investment thesis for a named short, and Plan A answers that question.
issues_with_winner: The methodology is dense (Driscoll–Kraay with 4 lags, affinity IV, multiple robustness specifications) and may not have clear off-the-shelf code; the analyst will need to implement or find obscure packages.
The permutation null is conceptually sound but operationally tricky—implementation bugs are easy and hard to spot, and the PM may not intuively trust the result even if it passes.

The IV strategy (national non-sports Kalshi volume × pre-period affinity to predict adoption) is somewhat circular: affinity is fit on the same pre-period window used to define W̄, risking weak instrument bias in finite samples.
The analyst must hand-audit 500 transactions and verify sportsbook-launched prediction market dates in filings, which is labor-intensive and error-prone.

The plan does not explicitly address differential attrition by cohort (Jan 2023 adopters retained at different rates than Jan 2025 adopters) in the pooled estimation, relying on balanced/unbalanced panel checks to catch it.
issues_with_loser: The core estimand (ATT: average effect of Kalshi adoption on post-period DK spending) does not directly answer the position-sizing question; a PM still needs to infer from 'adopters spend X less' to 'therefore DK shorts should be sized at Y.'

The causal claim rests entirely on matching on observables; the plan lists reverse causality (DK self-exclusion, DK-initiated limits) as a pitfall but does not resolve it—pre-trend checks can rule out selection on unobservables only if adoption is unforecastable, which it is not.

Cohort-by-calendar-month fixed effects absorb economy-wide shocks but also eat variation if cohorts are small; the plan specifies no minimum cohort size and does not bound the number of cohorts under which wild cluster bootstrap is conservative (literature suggests >30 for validity, and this plan says 'under 30, add wild bootstrap').

The propensity score is estimated on pre-period covariates (tenant, transaction count, DK dollar slope, inflow, etc.) but does not include pre-DK changes in propensity to adopt (e.g., has the user been searching for alternatives, opening accounts at competitors?), which is likely correlated with both adoption and post-period DK churn.

The plan prioritizes Type II error reduction (1:5 matching, 80% power MDE, partial identification bounds) which is backward for a concentrated short position; it will likely over-estimate the effect and build false conviction.

Matching within tight cohorts (<6, 6–12, 13–24, 25+ month tenure buckets) and state may leave very few eligible control-to-adopter pairs in small cohorts; the plan drops unmatched adopters but does not bound bias from the dropped set.
The event study is clean but standard; it provides no heterogeneity by pre-spend decile, tenure, or the tenure × spend interaction that Plan A highlights and that a PM would want for position-sizing.

result.key_differentiator: Plan B gates the fundamental proxy claim first and kills the idea if seats don't move with MAU, whereas Plan A runs sophisticated time-series work on the assumption that MAU measures the billed unit without ever validating that assumption.
result.rationale: Both plans address a mechanism question: does user engagement (MAU) predict billing (ARR) via seats? The error structure favors Type II dominance — a false negative (missing a real signal across many companies) costs more than a false positive (overweighting one relationship in position sizing), so a plan that gatekeeps early saves weeks of wasted time-series work if the premise fails. Plan A is technically superior in robustness — cointegration tests, error-correction forms, vendor-specific linear trends, Bai–Perron break detection — but it buries the critical question. It assumes MAU correlates to seats and runs to residuals smaller than sell-side dispersion without ever checking whether disclosed seat counts or growth rates align with panel MAU at all. Plan B opens with exactly that gate: β in [0.5, 1.5] and partial correlation ≥0.45, or stop. If Panel B fails that gate, Plan A's elaborate machinery is solving the wrong problem. Plan B also fits the firm better. A 30-person fundamental shop with three data people and one engineer will struggle to staff production-grade cointegration testing, Pesaran CD tests, and rolling-origin validation across 40 effective clusters. Plan B's simpler OLS with Driscoll–Kraay and block bootstrap is defensible to a PM in real time, and the output — a nowcast + five-day ahead growth forecast with explicit residual variance — plugs directly into position sizing. Plan A produces Diebold–Mariano p-values and MAPE ratios against benchmarks, which is good for publication but not actionable for named position sizing on a six-to-18-month horizon. Plan B also sequences for information. Weeks 1–2: does disclosed seat growth correlate with MAU growth? Kill or proceed. Weeks 3–4: validation, nowcasting, and regime splits. Plan A spends weeks 1–4 on data cleaning (panel composition, tracker re-basings, price-index snapshots), then runs all three horizons in parallel, then checks benchmarks, then asks whether the relationship even survives when MAU reverses (the shelfware test). The falsification check (refit on consumption-priced names) is clever but comes late and only works if the main sample survived. In principle Plan A's level work (absolute ARR forecasting with company trends) is harder and more valuable than Plan B's growth-rate work, but not if the premise — that MAU moves seats — fails. And for position sizing on a concentrated book, growth-rate nowcasts are actionable faster than level forecasts. Plan B names its kill criteria in advance (four simultaneous gates, all must pass) and makes them binary. Plan A lists pitfalls and proposes patches, but never says which combination of patches disqualifies the idea. Plan A is the better plan if you already know seats and MAU move together. Plan B is the better plan if you don't, which is the actual state of knowledge, and that is the job being asked.
issues_with_winner: Gate criterion (β in [0.5,1.5]) is tight and might reject a real effect if price per seat drifts; Plan B should report what happens at β=0.3 or β=2.0 before killing.

Growth-rate work is cleaner than level work, but it throws away the ARR-forecast opportunity; if the gate passes, Plan B should describe a path to conditional level modeling rather than stopping at growth nowcasts.

Ridge regression and empirical-Bayes shrinkage are less transparent to a PM than OLS, despite being more robust; Plan B should include an interpretable OLS benchmark alongside to explain to investors why shrinkage matters.

Validation relies on consensus-surprise outperformance (>55% sign hits), which is a low bar if consensus is stale; Plan B should specify how fresh consensus snapshots are and whether consensus ever knows about MAU.
issues_with_loser: Plan A runs level-ARR forecasting without first validating that MAU predicts seats, which is the fundamental question; if the gate fails, the entire time-series apparatus is wasted effort.

Pitfalls section names confounders (shelfware, price drift, panel composition, SSO underpanelling) but sequencing puts all of them after model estimation; Plan A should run the shelfware interaction and SSO-coverage check first, not as a post-hoc robustness check.

Demanding MAPE <3% and residuals smaller than sell-side dispersion implies Plan A expects to outforecast consensus as a byproduct; that is not stated as a gate and may not be achievable even if MAU genuinely predicts seats, if price volatility dominates.

Diebold–Mariano testing against level-forecast benchmarks requires very precise ARR denominations; Plan A's data section permits four splicing rules and three different ARR definitions, which creates degrees of freedom in benchmark comparison.

The plan assumes the analyst can operationalize 'cointegrated or not' and 'error-correction form or differenced' as a sequential filter; that is nontrivial and the guidance is sparse about when to pick which branch.

result.key_differentiator: Plan A gates on whether MAU is even a valid proxy for seats before building a nowcast; Plan B assumes this and builds a predictive model for a fund that cannot act on a general cross-sectional signal and needs to move position sizing on named companies.
result.rationale: This is fundamentally a single-name, position-sizing question for a long/short manager with a concentrated portfolio. The research question is: does this signal help us size ADP, Paycom, Atlassian, etc. better? Plan B misreads this entirely. It builds a pooled cross-sectional model predicting ARR one quarter ahead across 35–60 names, with validation focused on MAPE across the ensemble. That output answers "is there a general market-wide signal in MAU?" not "should we buy or sell Paycom at current prices?" A 15% RMSE reduction in a pooled model is worthless if it's driven by five large-cap names where the position is already crowded and the edge is zero. The PM cannot defend adding 2% to position size in a single name based on a pooled regression coefficient and Diebold–Mariano p-values. For a six-month holding horizon and concentrated decision-making, the manager needs to know: (1) is MAU actually measuring seat growth for this specific company or is it mostly showing pricing/contract-churn noise; (2) how much of ARR variance is seats versus price for *this* name; (3) if MAU is clean, what does the current quarter's read imply for next quarter's billings on a timescale they can act on. Plan A is built for exactly this. It gates first on the foundational question: does the relationship β=1 hold (MAU growth = seat growth) with sufficient stability? It does this within company with company fixed effects, not by pooling noise across an ensemble. It reports the variance decomposition per company—how much of ARR growth is seats versus price per name—so the analyst knows whether the signal even matters for this business. It explicitly kills the idea if the gate fails, which is the right outcome because a pooled β-hat that holds on average is useless if it is unreliable for the two names the fund owns. On the validation side, Plan A demands 90% bootstrap confidence intervals excluding zero, a partial correlation ≥0.45, and leave-one-out stability—much tighter than Plan B's threshold of "above consensus dispersion." This matters for Type I error. A concentrated long/short book with explicit loss and asymmetric downside cannot diversify away a false positive. If the analyst recommends a 4% position in Paycom based on a spurious MAU correlation—one that works in-sample but fails in the next cycle—the loss is asymmetric and material. Plan A's sequencing is also far better. It opens with the gate: does MAU-to-seat conversion work for this company at all? This is the highest-uncertainty, lowest-cost check. It winsorizes breaks, trends coverage ratios, inspects >25% moves by hand, and tests cointegration-style stability (leads/lags). Only on a pass does it move to the nowcast model. If the gate fails—which it will for some names (Dropbox has low portal adoption; Salesforce has massive non-seat revenue; Snowflake is consumption-metered)—the analyst learns within days and the work is killed without sunk cost. Plan B front-loads data integration and runs all 35–60 names through pooled estimation regardless. Coverage flags a problem: a 50% hold-one-company-out drop or a 30% coefficient swing is explained away as "edge decaying in smaller-cap names." This is loss aversion dressed as insight. For the firm's infrastructure, Plan A is more aligned. The data team can license Similarweb and mobile panels (they already do this). The analyst can do simple log-differencing, OLS with cluster SEs, and bootstrap—all bread-and-butter tools. The output is per-company variance decompositions and a nowcast model coefficients they can hand to the PM with a worked example. "Paycom's portal MAU grew 12% YoY; last three years, seat growth and MAU growth had a correlation of 0.58 and covariance consistent with β≈0.8. The prior quarter MAU + one-year price momentum imply 8% ARR growth next quarter, versus sell-side at 6%." That is defensible and actionable. The PM can ask what would have to be true for it to be wrong: "If Paycom's price-per-seat rises faster than we expect, or if seats are contracting while portal users stay flat, the signal fails." Plan B's output is a pooled model p-value and a MAPE across 40 companies, some of which the fund does not own. The PM will ask what the coefficient means for Asana specifically. The analyst cannot answer without redoing the leave-one-out test on that one name. Plan A is not perfect. The gate thresholds are specific and could be gamed (post-hoc tuning of the >0.15 coverage SD or the 0.45 partial correlation). The Driscoll–Kraay SE with Newey–West lag 4 is reasonable for quarterly data but assumes weak cross-sectional dependence in a small sample of names; the diagnostic for this (Pesaran CD) is not listed. If seat disclosure and portal MAU share a common macro trend (both slack during recessions), the within-company fixed-effects model could absorb the causality, and the lagged dependent variable in the nowcast model (with ridge regularization) is a hedge against spurious fit. The empirical Bayes shrinkage could suppress real heterogeneity. These are manageable. Plan B's issues are structural. The premise of pooling 35–60 names is that the relationship is stable cross-sectionally, but it opens with the observation that MAU-per-seat and price-per-seat drift slowly—i.e., they are heterogeneous and time-varying. Fitting a single β across such heterogeneity, then validating on hold-one-company-out, does not measure whether the signal is useful for a single-name decision. The falsification test (refit on consumption-metered names) is clever but backwards: if the effect does exist for seat-metered names, it should *not* work for consumption names, so equal performance would argue the signal is something else (macro, growth, quality) not specific to the proposed mechanism. The rolling-origin test is sound but comes late, after tuning on the 20% holdout. The 150 bps median absolute error threshold in year-over-year growth is vague—relative to what baseline, and is 150 bps tolerable for a 6-month position? The plan does not say. The price index control from Wayback snapshots is brittle; subscription tier pricing changes often and irregularly (an enterprise version launched, an SMB tier discontinued), so the scalar log-price index conflates products. And most consequentially, the PM cannot extract a single-name trade: the model gives a cross-sectional prediction, not a per-company nowcast adjusted for firm-specific proxy validity. Plan A's primary weakness—its reliance on hand inspection and case-by-case gating—is actually a strength in this context. A concentrated manager needs to know why the signal works for some names and not others. Plan B's attempt at scale and statistical completeness is misapplied here. The question is not whether a signal exists in a panel; it is whether it moves the needle on named positions, and only Plan A is structured to answer that.
issues_with_winner: The gate thresholds (90% CI excluding zero, partial correlation ≥0.45, β̂ in [0.5, 1.5]) are specific and could be post-hoc-tuned; Pesaran CD test for cross-sectional dependence is mentioned in pitfalls but not pre-committed to the gate.
The empirical Bayes shrinkage in the nowcast model adds a layer of estimation that could suppress real company-level heterogeneity, particularly for smaller or newer companies.
Driscoll–Kraay with Newey–West lag 4 assumes weak cross-sectional dependence in a small sample of 15–25 names; the true dependence (through tech macro shocks, indexing rebalances) is not modeled.
The lagged dependent variable in the nowcast (Δ₄ln(ARR)_{t−1}) is a hedge against spuriousness but, combined with fixed effects and ridge regularization, could soak up signal.
Hand-inspection of >25% breaks and coverage drift is labor-intensive and relies on the analyst's judgment; no objective threshold for when to exclude a company is stated upfront.
issues_with_loser: Pooling 35–60 names conflates heterogeneous relationships; the model cannot distinguish between names where MAU is a strong proxy for seats and names where it is noise, so single-name position sizing is not supported.
Validation gates on "above consensus dispersion in ≥60% of quarters," which is a low bar; consensus dispersion is itself often a sign of uncertainty, not a reliable anchor for the true error.

The falsification test (consumption-metered names) is backwards: if MAU predicts ARR via a seats mechanism, it should *not* work for consumption names, so equal performance would confirm the signal is something else (macro, growth, quality), not refute the premise.
Rolling-origin validation comes late, after tuning on the 20% holdout; the holdout is used to choose horizon and model form, which is a mild form of researcher degrees of freedom.

The price control is fragile: log price index from Wayback snapshots conflates product-mix changes (new enterprise tier, discontinued SMB tier) and cannot capture pricing power or negotiation changes.

Output is pooled coefficients and MAPE ratios, not per-company nowcasts; the PM cannot extract a trade recommendation for a specific name without redoing left-one-out or querying the analyst for firm-specific residuals.
The 150 bps median absolute error bar in YoY growth is stated without a baseline or loss function; is that good relative to persistence, or relative to the manager's rebalancing frequency?
The mechanism statement ("MAU-per-seat and price-per-seat drifting slowly") is noted but never tested; heterogeneity in drift across names is not modeled or checked.

The paper does not address whether the signal decays quickly (implied by "expect edge in smaller-cap names, decaying"); if decay is fast, the lead time from quarterly MAU to quarterly ARR may be too long to act on for a six-month horizon.

result.key_differentiator: Plan B is built to solve the actual problem — a defensible filter with precision guarantees and known failure modes — while Plan A addresses a different question: whether unsupervised clustering reveals institution structure.
result.rationale:
The desk has one need: a filter that keeps only Visa-first European banks, dropping the rest, that a PM can defend to auditors and trading counterparties. Both plans try to identify institutions from transaction fingerprints, but they answer different questions and impose different burdens of proof.

Plan A is a discovery project dressed as a filter. It assumes that good clustering on behavioral features will reveal true institutions, naming them only after clusters emerge. Silhouette >0.40 and Jaccard >0.60 signal coherent clusters, but coherence is not correctness — a Plan A cluster might be all the neobanks of Western Europe, or all young-professional users across 12 institutions. The plan names institutions by feeding good clusters through a constrained assignment: match cluster profiles to market-share ranks, then assign via Hungarian algorithm. This works if clusters align with true institutions. But the null hypothesis — that IDs differ only by size and demographic mix — is weak. Real failure, the plan admits in pitfalls, is confusing account role (primary vs savings) with institution identity, or identifying sub-brands and BINs as separate institutions when they are not. Plan A has no way to know whether its tier-A institutions are real or phantoms. It validates stability (resampling, windows, permutation tests) but never validates correctness against ground truth. The plan mentions hand-reading 20 narratives per cluster as a final gate, but a PM cannot defend a filter built on 20 customer stories, and the plan offers no scoring rule that ties naming to confidence. If pressed on why a cluster should be believed, Plan A has no answer except "it was stable and separated."

Plan B is built as a filter with precision guarantees. It defines the actual target upfront: institutions identified at ≥95% precision on held-out institutions, and by country, only if ≥40% of deposit volume can be assigned. It fixes a killing criterion: if the Netherlands fails (the easiest market, most concentrated, highest-quality anchors), stop. It uses ground truth. Validation is leave-one-institution-out on labeled data (consented survey, provider-revealed seeds, public cases: 25–60 per country) with nested CV to avoid threshold overfitting. It reports precision, recall, coverage unweighted and volume-weighted, and a risk–coverage curve. A PM can defend a precision threshold: "We accept only institutions where ≥95% of transactions we assign actually belong to that institution," and if that threshold cannot be met, the filter abstains (marks UNKNOWN) rather than guessing. The plan ties confidence (Sinkhorn marginals, Venn–Abers calibration) to output. It rehearses failure: permuted fingerprints must score at chance, phantom IDs must abstain, dropping the largest comparator must degrade gracefully.

On firm fit: The desk is long/short fundamental with 30 investment staff, not a machine-learning team. It licensed one panel and does not trust it. It has one data engineer and a small core data team. It needs something it can explain to a PM, and something that fails loudly rather than quietly. Plan A requires iterative tuning of k, robustness thresholds, rubric rules (e.g., "neobank = under-30 >35%"), and rescaling on within-country distributions. It is a machine-learning project that generates many intermediate artifacts (PCA loadings, co-association matrices, UMAP plots) but no precision guarantee. A PM will ask "What breaks if we use this filter?" and Plan A's answer is "It is stable across resamples and six-month windows." That is not reassuring.

Plan B is an econometric identification problem. It uses anchors (the ECB register, branch directories, tariff databases, benefit calendars) as external truth. It is explicit about what it validates and what remains unknown. It also sequences better: it pilots the Netherlands first, a market where identification should be easy. If it fails there, the whole effort stops. Plan A runs the full pipeline and only at the end, through hand-reading 20 narratives, asks whether names are plausible.

On error asymmetry: Type I error dominates. A filter that quietly admits a non-Visa-first bank, or one controlled by a sponsor bank that is not EU-regulated, is a show-stopper. The downside is asymmetric and explicit: the fund's PMs could build research and positioning on a compromised dataset. Plan A offers stability and internal coherence but no precision bound. Plan B offers a precision threshold, holdout testing on labeled data, and an abstain option.

On sequencing and information: Plan A buries the crucial question — does clustering give true institutions or account roles? — in the pitfalls section and proposes a remedy (re-cluster on primary accounts if role is the issue) only after the full pipeline runs. Plan B asks the hard question first: get labeled data (500 surveys, provider seeds, public cases), and pilot in the simplest market (Netherlands). If those fail, the project stops. Plan B also adapts: if Sinkhorn marginals show a near-tie, it abstains rather than picking a name; if anchor vintage is suspect, it versions quarterly.

On simplicity and defensibility: Plan B is the simpler claim. Fingerprints + anchors + labeled validation = identifiable. Plan A is more elaborate — six types of clustering, co-association reconciliation, permutation importance, gradient-boosted naming rubric — but rests on an untested leap from stability to truth.

Plan A's strengths: It is thoughtful about confounders (role, whitespace, reweighting for panel skew, seasonal adjustment). It validates stability rigorously. It produces pictures (UMAP) and interpretable features (salary detection, ATM intensity). It would serve well as a **exploratory phase** to understand institution-like structure in the data.

Plan A's fatal flaw: It has no way to know whether the names are correct. A PM will not sign off on a filter built on unsupervised clustering, no matter how stable, without precision validation on held-out ground truth.

Plan B's strengths: Precision-first design, labeled validation, nested holdout, abstain option, pilot-and-kill gate, adapted thresholds, volume-weighted metrics, explicit failure modes.

Plan B's weakness: It requires labeled data (500 surveys per country is a real lift), and it depends on anchor quality (ECB register, branch directories, tariffs). Tariffs vary by country and vintage; some banks do not publish PLVs; OSM coverage is patchy. But these are engineering risks, not conceptual ones. Plan B explicitly flags them ("anchor vintage amid consolidation") and proposes versioning. And the plan is honest: if you cannot get labeled data, you cannot validate identification, period. Plan A hides that problem by calling stability "validation."

On the desk's single actual need — a filter that keeps Visa-first European banks and drops the rest, defensible to a PM — Plan B answers it. Plan A answers "Here is a machine-learning model that finds structure in the data," which is different and not useful without precision guarantees.

result.key_differentiator: Plan A directly answers the filter question with a defensible pass/fail per institution; Plan B solves the harder problem of naming institutions without proving it can separate signal from noise well enough to filter safely.
result.rationale:
The desk's actual need is a filter: keep transactions from Visa-first European banks, drop the rest. This is a binary classification problem per institution with asymmetric cost — admitting a non-bank or regional bank is silent contamination of the research dataset; discarding a real bank wastes panel volume but is detectable. Plan A is built for exactly this gate function. It names a precision criterion (≥95%) fixed in advance, establishes a coverage floor (≥40% per country), sequences the kill criterion first (governance/GDPR), and produces per-institution acceptance verdicts (`ACCEPT`/`UNKNOWN`) with coded failure reasons that a PM can audit. The validation is institution-level leave-one-out — the right unit — with explicit negative controls (permuted fingerprints, phantom IDs). Precision-weighted by deposit volume makes sense because large institutions matter more to the fund's exposures. The method is sophisticated but the output is binary and defensible: "We identified 47 Dutch institutions at ≥95% precision across 2.1M customers; we held out 8 and retained ≥94% on each; 23 are Visa-first and in scope."

Plan B solves a different, harder problem: clustering 150–400 institutions into business-model archetypes and naming them. This is useful research, but it does not answer the filter question. The desk needs to know whether an opaque ID is a bank they should keep, not whether it is a neobank, incumbent, or cooperative. Even if Plan B's clustering were perfect, naming IDs via gradient-boosted classifier on pre-PCA features + constrained Hungarian matching introduces a new validation gap: does the classifier reliably separate signal from noise? The method says "accept only if ≤3 candidates, ranks agree, top-to-runner-up gap clears preset margin" — but those thresholds are tuned inside the same sample that built the classifier. Plan B's validation is cluster-stability (Jaccard >0.75 on resampled customers, ARI >0.60 across six-month windows, Silhouette >0.40) and null-beating (vs. permuted customers) — all reasonable tests of whether clusters are real — but none of these directly measure whether the gradient-boosted naming classifier is right. A cluster can be statistically stable and still be mislabeled. Plan B also reports Tier C ("named candidate set") as a usable output; the desk cannot act on a candidate set without manual investigation, which reintroduces the human labor the panel was supposed to replace.

Firm fit also favors Plan A. The fund has three data-team people who clean panels and one engineer. Plan A's infrastructure is heavy (ECB RIAD/MFI quarterly joins, CBD2/national-regulator reconciliation, Overpass OSM scraping, tariff harmonization, Sinkhorn/Jonker–Volgenant, nested CV, Venn–Abers calibration) but it is *one* deployed filter that lives in the codebase and runs monthly on new transaction batches. Plan B requires maintaining an evolving taxonomy (country, archetype, institution name), clustering logic that drifts with seasonal and structural changes, and hand-reading 20-customer narratives per cluster iteration — that is operational overhead a three-person team will struggle to own. Plan B explicitly notes "hand-read 20 random customers' twelve-month narratives per top-five cluster; verdict before signature," which on a rolling panel is not scalable.

Error asymmetry also tips the scale. Admitting a non-bank (Type I) means downstream research runs on contaminated data — subtle, silent, affects many analyses. Discarding a real bank (Type II) is noticed immediately (lower panel volume in one country) and recoverable (manual audit of marginal cases). Type I dominates; Plan A's ≥95% precision threshold is the right burden, and Plan B's stability/silhouette gates do not directly control precision.

Sequencing also matters. Plan A kills the work at gate zero if governance fails (GDPR, licence, regulator sign-off); Plan B treats governance as a buried pitfall. For alt-data in a regulated asset class, that is a material difference.

Plan A has real issues. The sophistication of the scoring function (log-likelihood ratios, Jensen–Shannon divergence, Wasserstein distance, min-cost flow) requires implementation care; a bug in the min-cost routing or logistic mapping could silently degrade precision. The anchor data (tariffs, benefit calendars, growth disclosures) must be kept current and harmonized across five countries — the ECB/DNB/Banco de España sources are quarterly, but Kindergeld and AOW calendars do not update every quarter. If tariff data is stale or incomplete, the fee-signature feature will add noise. The survey labels are small (25–60 per country; Netherlands may be <30) and drawn from a self-selected cohort; if respondents skew toward large/well-known banks, the precision on small regional banks will not be validated. The permuted-fingerprint null is a good sanity check, but it does not catch subtle correlations (e.g., if payday and fee signature are mechanically correlated through institution size, permuting only fingerprints may not catch the leak).

Plan B has worse issues for this task. The gradient-boosted classifier that produces the final names is trained and validated on the same cluster assignments from the same data; if those clusters are (say) conflating two institutions that serve identical demographics in different countries, the classifier will learn to name them apart anyway, and the out-of-fold Jaccard/ARI/silhouette tests will not catch it. The archetype rubric ("neobank: under-30 >35%, new accounts >25%, ATM outflow <5%") is pre-committed but not validated — if the panel skews young, a savings bank with many young customers will score as neobank-like. Plan B explicitly notes this ("Panel skews young/urban/digital/multi-banked, inflating neobanks, under-representing cooperative/regional banks: use panel-reweighted shares; state bias") but reweighting does not unbiass the clustering; it just re-centers the mean. The NMF co-holding loadings (k=6–10) add degrees of freedom for overfitting; the choice of k is not described as data-driven or pre-committed. The hand-reading validation (20 customers per cluster, "verdict before signature") is a gut check, not a systematic validation; it will catch obvious mislabeling but not subtle contamination (e.g., a second-bank-for-savings account flagged as primary).

The desk asked: "Can we reliably identify European financial institutions from transaction data?" Plan A directly answers this with a precision floor, institution-by-institution verdicts, and a kill criterion. Plan B answers the adjacent question "Can we cluster and name institutions by business model?" which is more ambitious and, for the desk's immediate purpose, unnecessary. The fund's stated pain point is "a filter nobody can vouch for" — Plan A produces something a PM can inspect and defend; Plan B produces a taxonomy that requires hand-verification at scale. Given the firm's constraints (small data team, need for maintainability, horizon of 6–18 months to deploy), Plan A is the right work.

result.key_differentiator: Plan A treats this as a statistical hypothesis test on a population of comparables; Plan B recognizes this is a single-name legal and document-forensics question where the binding constraint is whether this specific release happened, for what stated reason, and what economic substitutes replaced it.
result.rationale:
Plan A is a well-designed population study that would be valuable to a systematic firm asking whether guarantor exits signal strategic re-sourcing *on average across semiconductors and project finance*. It is not this. This desk does single-name deep-dive work with an event-driven catalyst and weeks-to-months horizon. The goal is binary: is *this* situation mispriced right now, not whether an effect replicates. Plan A's architecture — comparative case studies, base-rate estimation, hypothesis coding across 40–60 comparables, H-stat testing at 25:1 LR threshold — is methodologically sound but answers the wrong question. It takes eight weeks minimum and produces a population-level inference ('mechanical releases dominate 20:1 to 30:1, therefore this one is probably ordinary') on a setting where one document amendment, one consent solicitation form, or one supplier qualification announcement ends the argument. It also assumes the desk can staff this work; they have two analysts and no quant research capacity, and a 40-comparable study is not their operational model. Plan A imports the research infrastructure and statistical culture of a systematic shop into a fundamental event-driven one.

Plan B starts with the right sequence: kill the scheduled-release hypothesis (H2) first by reading the documents themselves — Completion/COD definitions, DSCR test thresholds, release conditions as-signed. If H2 holds, the guarantor exit is irrelevant strategically and the work stops. Only if H2 dies does the analysis move to risk-transfer mechanisms (H3) and then strategic re-sourcing (H1). This is entropy-reducing order. The plan is designed for the person it is written for: someone with legal-document expertise and expert networks, short horizon, and capacity to make yes/no calls on whether forms match their terms. It names explicit falsifiers — release language matching schedule, no consent solicitation, no qualification predating the change — and structures them as kill criteria, which is how this desk works. The second-source validation is modest and corroborated through multiple channels (IP licensing, OSAT orders, hiring, EDA vendor disclosures, channel work) rather than statistically. The price-reaction check ('check first') is the kind of market-sense reality test this desk does. The output is a bridge, a dated timeline, a verdict, and if H1 holds, a trade sized to weakness, which is what a PM needs.

Plan B also names the right confounders for this context: antitrust review, FDI screening, export control, transfer pricing — these are the reasons a guarantor might exit that have nothing to do with sourcing strategy. A PM on this desk will know these matter more than hiring patterns do. Plan B's caveat about dual sourcing coexisting with incumbent growth is operationally smart: it tells the analyst how to think about the interpretation before the money is deployed, not as a retrospective pitfall.

Both plans acknowledge their pitfalls. Plan A lists them (legal form vs economics, anchoring, timing illusion) but then proceeds as if they do not exist — the guarantee-release trigger might be scheduled, but the comparable-rate coding will still treat it as signal unless Plan B's falsifiers hold, which are then gated behind an eight-week statistical analysis. Plan B puts the falsifiers first and makes them decision-points, not caveats.

Plan A is methodologically sophisticated and would be publishable. It is not suited to this firm or this question. Plan B is designed for a one-name event-driven desk with legal expertise and a short clock, and it has the right operative sequence and decision gates.
issues_with_winner: Relies on manual channel work (OSAT/IEDM papers/job postings/counsel calls) that is real but not scalable; if the qualification evidence is mixed or ambiguous, the verdict is harder to commit. Plan B implicitly trusts the analyst's judgment at endpoints where Plan A would want numbers.

Does not fully address how to disagree with counsel if documents are ambiguous; the 'ASC 810 test did not happen' observation lives downstream of the guarantee check, leaving some interpretive risk. Plan A's comparative logic would resolve this by base-rate, albeit slowly.

Redaction back-solving is proposed but not detailed; if the SPV is tightly redacted for market-access reasons, the debt quantum and DSCR can remain opaque, leaving the leverage-transfer thesis incompletely verified.

The 5–10 base-rate comparables for validation are informal; if this vintage of sponsor-supported SPV has different release practices than Plan A suggests, the falsification logic may not hold. Plan B assumes the analyst's primary sources outweigh aggregate patterns, which is usually right but can be wrong.
issues_with_loser: Answers a population-level question when the goal is single-name. For a one-name desk with weeks to a decision, an eight-week study producing 'guarantor exits are usually scheduled' (even with 25:1 LR) arrives after the trade has moved or the market has priced it.

Violates entropy-reducing sequencing: it proposes 40–60 case studies across three strata before it has confirmed whether the original SPV's release was scheduled or negotiated. The most glaring check (do the documents say the release was automatic?) is buried in comparables-coding work rather than placed first.

Assumes infrastructure the firm does not have: comparative case-study coding, LR hypothesis testing, databases of comparables (DealScan, Infralogic, Bloomberg CACS), and time to calibrate these. This desk does primary-source and expert work, not database-driven population analysis. The plan's data section lists 8–10 databases; the firm likely has only three (EDGAR, TWSE MOPS, Bloomberg generic). Acquiring the rest and building a coding scheme is spend not justified when a document read could kill the idea.

Over-elaborates on legal form classification (40–60 coded triggers, distinguishing scheduled/negotiated, accounting vs leverage-driven) when the single question is: did this specific guarantee release meet its pre-written trigger? The coding taxonomy is methodologically sound but operationally wasteful for a one-name case.

Makes the falsification test dependent on prior-art dominance ('mechanical/refinancing dominate 20:1–30:1'); if the base rate is actually 3:1 or 1:1, the inference inverts. The comparable-rate estimates are presented as prior facts rather than things to update on, which is backwards. This desk would rightly ask 'yes, but in what sub-segment and does that sub-segment match us?' and Plan A does not prepare to answer that.

Positions hiring/IP/reticle-customs evidence ('OSAT/packaging-site/second-vendor HBM qualification, available packaging capacity; hiring reqs naming rival PDK, node, DFM flow') as something to be coded across 60 cases rather than as something to validate directly on the two names involved. The plan does not clearly separate 'signal we care about (independent qualification) done by inference' from 'signal done by direct observation.' If one foundry shows qualification, Plan B finds it; Plan A would require it to replicate across 60 cases before it counts.

result.key_differentiator: Plan A sequences the question for speed and defensibility in a single-name event-driven setting with asymmetric downside; Plan B is built for systematic signal validation and cannot fail fast.
result.rationale:
This is a single-name mispricing question for a concentrated event-driven desk with a few-month horizon and two analysts. The goal is not to establish whether an effect exists across many cases, but to resolve one specific situation well enough to size a position right now.

Plan A is purpose-built for this firm and this question. It opens with the null hypotheses ranked by disconfirmation cost and names the cheapest kill first—document review proving scheduled release language kills H1 immediately without any fieldwork. It treats the second source as a corroboration step rather than a statistical proof point, acknowledges that primary sources are imperfect and need triangulation across documents and channels, and outputs a dated timeline and a trade size keyed to the weakest link. The work is inspectable at each stage: a PM can read the release language herself, trace the argument through the credit agreement and guarantee articles, and evaluate whether the qualification evidence is independent. The plan is honest about what redactions hide and names an explicit workaround. Most critically, it knows what would kill the idea and when—this desk needs to walk away from a theory by week two if the documents are unambiguous, not discover in week eight that a scheduled release made the whole analysis moot.

Plan B is a cross-sectional signal-design plan dressed up as single-name research. It codes forty to sixty comparables, tests a statistical hypothesis that "mechanical/refinancing dominate, 20:1–30:1 against H1," pre-registers falsifiers, runs a portfolio sweep across eight quarters of footnotes, and indexes to a prior base rate. All of this is sophisticated and appropriate for answering the question "how often do guarantor exits signal second-source qualification across semiconductor and infrastructure?" That is not this question. This desk does not need a Bayesian update from comparables; it needs to know whether *this* one is mispriced. Using forty comparables to calibrate a prior for one name is the wrong inference problem for someone who can afford to spend two weeks on primary documents.

On firm fit, Plan B assumes infrastructure that does not exist here. It requires access to DealScan, Infralogic/IJGlobal, Bloomberg CACS/DDIS, MOPS, DART, EDINET, UCC databases, and months of coding work across institutional data sources. The desk has no quant staff, no dataset-building capacity, and no reason to license infrastructure for a single position. It consumes sell-side, filings, and expert networks. Plan A uses only documents the hyperscaler and manufacturer are required to disclose, plus counsel conversations and channel work the desk already does. The output of Plan B—a falsified hypothesis and a Bayesian posterior—is useful to a systematic firm sizing an allocation across many positions. The output of Plan A—"release language is unambiguous, here is the timeline, here is where we would look for second-source evidence, here is what would kill it"—is what a PM on an event-driven desk actually uses to size a position.

On error asymmetry, this desk cannot diversify. A false positive on a concentrated bet is an explicit, asymmetric loss. A false negative—discarding a real mispricing because the documents were ambiguous or second-source evidence was scarce—caps upside but does not create a loss; they simply do not take the position. The burden of proof should be high and the disconfirmation path should be cheap. Plan A meets this by naming the killing conditions upfront and testing them first. Plan B does the reverse: it accumulates evidence over months against a statistical hypothesis, which means false positives survive longer and cost more.

On sequencing, Plan A gets to 60% confidence in weeks and stops if the documents kill it. Plan B is not scheduled to produce anything actionable until the comparable analysis is coded—a month or more away—and even then requires synthesis across six different kill conditions, any two of which are supposed to falsify H1. That is weakly motivated: two of the six falsifiers are "field evidence shows no qualification" or "incumbent volumes rose," which are the same fact looked at from different sides and should not independently drive the verdict. The comparable-code-first approach also inverts entropy: the most glaring check (what does the actual legal document say?) is scheduled late, after months of infrastructure work and coding.

Plan A is not perfect. The document list is encyclopedic and some items (fixture filings, presale reports, UCC-1s) are secondary to the core question. The write-up assumes comfort with corporate-finance jargon that the PM may not have; a good analyst would need to simplify on delivery. The plan does not explicitly name how long the field work takes or what happens if the second source is rumored but not yet public. And it may underestimate the power of seeing the base rate: forty comparables is not nothing, and an analyst who codes them might learn patterns that sharp document reading alone would miss.

But Plan B has a deeper flaw. It assumes the question is "how probable is second-source qualification given a guarantor exit?" The real question is "is this specific exit a sign of second-source qualification, and should we position accordingly?" Those are not the same. If the answer to the first is "one in thirty cases," the posterior given the documents and channel evidence could still be 90%, and the desk should trade. Plan B would spend two months establishing that one in thirty is the right base rate, then pivot to expensive fieldwork to update it. Plan A would spend two weeks running the fieldwork against a much less ambitious null—do the documents rule it out, and is there any independent evidence of qualification?—and save the month.

For a single-name desk with a short horizon and asymmetric downside, Plan A is the plan that actually matches the question and the firm. Plan B is the plan for a systematic research group sizing a long-term allocation, or a quant team validating a new signal. This is neither of those.

result.key_differentiator: Plan B prioritizes the specific effect claim and kill criteria early with a cheap, defensible test; Plan A builds elaborate infrastructure before validating whether the core effect clears the confidence bar this firm requires.
result.rationale:
Both plans understand the domain well and are written for a systematic firm. Both are competent. Plan A is more sophisticated and complete — the domain-adapted language model, multi-head classification, careful speaker-tag parsing, and comprehensive robustness suite are technically excellent. Plan B is simpler: Loughran-McDonald dictionary, pooled panel regression, pre-registered around seven lines of research. The choice turns on goal alignment, sequencing, and cost-benefit within this firm's structure.

Goal clarity: The question is whether sentiment predicts peer-relative outperformance broadly, not whether it can be measured at all. This is a broad-market-effect question, not a capability build. The error asymmetry here favors Type II (false negatives are expensive; a capped downside with breadth). For this combination, the right move is entropy reduction first: establish whether the core effect exists and clears the confidence bar before investing in measurement infrastructure.

Plan B's sequencing is built for learning. Days 1–3 establish the priors: Price-Doran-Peterson-Bliss and follow-ups show the effect was real (2004–2010). McLean-Pontiff and vendor survey calibrate the decay and crowding assumption. Only then does it commit (frozen pre-registration). Days 4–10 run the simplest specification that could work: LM tone, within-firm change, peer-relative return, standard controls, two-way clustering, Fama-MacBeth. It places the kill criterion front and center: a t-statistic of 2.5 clustered, rising to 2.9 by Bonferroni. Pass that gate, and a PM can act on days 11–14; fail it, and a two-page memo names the residual hypothesis (audio affect) without weeks wasted on towers of machinery.

Plan A's sequencing is completion-driven. It builds the language model (1.5–2B tokens, domain-adaptive MLM, two-headed fine-tuning on 6,000 hand-annotated sentences, 150k silver labels) before the regression. It is not wrong — the model quality controls and ablations are well-designed — but the order presumes the core effect is real. If the LM-generated tone signal does not beat LM-McDonald in a simple regression by day 8, Plan A has burned researcher-weeks and compute on feature engineering that could have been skipped.

For a systematic firm with a replication platform and research committee, this matters acutely. Their job is to re-run the finding independently. Plan B's frozen specification — tone measure, universe, peers, controls, standard errors — is defensible and replicable by the committee on their own infrastructure in days. Plan A's specification is tied to a fine-tuned DeBERTa and codebook-bootstrapped silver labels; replication requires that apparatus, and the research committee will not re-train the LM. If the LM-based alpha is genuinely better, the committee can verify it, but it becomes a production-infrastructure decision (should this enter screening?), not a research decision. For a fast signal that clears the bar, Plan B's output is actionable faster.

Crowding and decay: Both plans acknowledge decay. Plan B front-loads the vendor survey (S&P Global, MarketPsych, RavenPack, Bloomberg, AlphaSense, Aiera, etc. — it names seat costs and client counts). If tone is already licensed and traded by a dozen vendors, the signal is likely crowded. Plan B will know this by day 3 and avoid wasting weeks. Plan A lists "Possible zero: a clean null is a real output" in pitfalls but does not gate on it; it will finish the LM and report the null, which is correct, but later.

Error asymmetry: On a signal-development question with capped downside (the firm's worst case is "this does not work, move on") and unbounded upside (a clean effect + capacity), Type II errors are expensive. Plan B's gate of t > 2.5 is appropriate for a broad effect that has already been published and decayed; it does not demand post-Bonferroni rigor (t > 3.0 would be over-conservative here). Plan A's Harvey-Liu-Zhu t > 3.0 criterion is more stringent and acknowledges the multiple testing (ablations, peer definitions, sector variants), but that machinery exists to earn the criterion, not to set it. For the question "does the effect exist?" after a decade of prior work showing decay, Plan B's framework is better-matched.

Validation and falsification: Plan B pre-commits four kill criteria and runs them by day 10. (1) Tone t ≥ 2.5 clustered. (2) Net Sharpe and IR. (3) Sign correct in 7+ of 10 years, t > 2.0 excluding COVID. (4) Effect does not concentrate in tiny illiquid names. If any fails, the idea dies at day 14. Plan A's validation is stronger in detail (walk-forward, sector/year stability, reliability diagrams, ECE) but it is not gated — all the work happens regardless. Plan B's design is adaptive; Plan A's is a task list.

Infrastructure: Plan A assumes the firm will build and maintain a domain-adaptive LM plus multi-head classification pipeline. For a 200-person quant shop with production ML infrastructure, this is doable, but it is not cost-free. Plan B assumes the firm can parse transcripts (using StreetEvents or Capital IQ with WRDS) and run panel regressions. Vastly lower barrier. If the effect is real, the firm can always upgrade to the LM; if it is not, they have not sunk the cost.

Issues with Plan A: (1) Sequencing: builds the measurement apparatus before validating the core effect. (2) Cost commitment: domain-adaptive pretraining locks in researcher-weeks and compute before the gate. (3) Replicability for the research committee: the LM is a black box to them; they will evaluate the alpha, not the model. (4) No pre-committed kill criterion; list of pitfalls does not block execution if the effect looks weak. (5) If tone is already crowded (likely, given a decade of published work and vendor licensing), the fine-tuned LM will not recover an edge; Plan A will still finish and report a null.

Issues with Plan B: (1) Simplicity is a liability if the effect is truly there but LM-McDonald misses it; the firm will abandon the line early. (2) Pre-registration is only enforceable if the firm is disciplined (common in quant shops but not universal). (3) No ablations or speaker-tag logic; if the effect is hiding in CFO guidance vs. CEO tone, Plan B might miss it. (4) Capacity and infrastructure checks ("pass: days 11–14 build scope") are deferred; if the signal is real but too narrow, that becomes a week-12 realization. (5) LM-McDonald tone is relatively crude; if the edge lies in unscripted Q&A nuance (as Plan A hypothesizes), Plan B's dictionary misses it.

The margin: Plan B's pre-commit to kill criteria at t > 2.5 is defensible for a broad signal that has already decayed. Plan A's t > 3.0 is more stringent, but the work required to reach it is also vastly more expensive. For a systematic firm focused on capacity and crowding, Plan B's early-exit design and vendor-licensing survey is the higher-EV move. If the effect were novel and narrowly measurable (e.g., audio affect on insider trading), Plan A's precision would win; here, the effect is broad-but-decayed, and Plan B's cut is better. Confidence is moderate (3) because Plan A is genuinely competent and the firm can afford both; the choice is about sequencing philosophy and risk-adjusted return on research hours, not quality of execution.
