result.key_differentiator: Plan A matches a systematic firm's actual workflow and decision gate; Plan B solves a different problem (whether sentiment predicts returns generally) using methods that don't fit this firm's infrastructure or the information asymmetry available to it.
result.rationale: This is a systematic trading firm with 200 quants, tick-level data, and a production research platform that replays everything. The question is whether sentiment predicts peer-relative outperformance—a signal-generation problem, not a capability-build or mechanism test. Plan A is built for exactly this firm and problem. Plan B is built for an academic or asset-manager asking "does sentiment really matter" and trying to publish a generalizable finding. Signature tells: Plan A opens with vendor calls and published decay curves, establishing whether the idea is already crowded and what the prior should be. It pre-registers in git on day three before touching returns. It names explicit kill thresholds—a t of 2.1 fails it, capacity must clear 3% annualized net, sign must hold in 7 of 10 years. These are not arbitrary: a systematic firm dies on crowding and decay, so those gates come first. Plan A asks 'is this tradeable' and structures the entire investigation around that constraint. Plan B asks 'is this real' and builds infrastructure to answer it comprehensively. The NLP pipeline in Plan B is sophisticated—domain-adaptive BERT, speaker-role parsing, hedging and evasion detection, walk-forward validation on out-of-time test sets. None of this is wrong in isolation. But it commits weeks to building a proprietary tone model when the firm could license S&P or RavenPack and spend those weeks on the signal itself. More critically, Plan B does not establish crowding or decay before building the model. It proposes a November 2025 completion timeline (domain adaptation is 2–3 epochs on 2B tokens, gold annotation is 6k sentences + arbitration, model development and ablation is sequential), whereas Plan A produces a kill/go decision by day 14. For a systematic firm, early failure is valuable—if the idea is arbitraged, establish that in two weeks, not ten. Plan B's error asymmetry is also wrong for this setting. The firm has limited capital and must redeploy constantly; a false positive is expensive (crowding, capacity limits, decay). Plan B treats false negatives as the costly error—it demands a t of 3.0, builds Bayesian uncertainty into the model, runs extensive robustness checks—which is appropriate for deciding whether to publish or change a portfolio construction view. It is not appropriate for deciding whether to burn a month of analyst time on a signal that might already be sold by a vendor. Plan A's t of 2.5 rising to 2.9 for multiple tests is tighter than publication standard but looser than Plan B, matching a firm that needs to move fast and can live with a modest false-positive rate as long as it does not trap capital. Firm fit is decisive here. Plan A names Russell 3000 point-in-time via WRDS and Capital IQ transcripts, which this firm has. It works within the production platform (replicating is the final gate). Plan B requires Xpressfeed/Snowflake access and assumes the firm can build and retrain a domain-adapted transformer. The firm almost certainly can technically, but the opportunity cost is too high—a 200-quant systematic shop does not staff up proprietary NLP when the question is signal generation, not model building. Plan B's assumption is that the firm wants to own the tone measurement for reasons of secrecy or edge. That is not what a systematic firm buying earnings-call data in 2025 believes. By now, tone is a solved technical problem; the edge is in discovering what tone actually predicts that others have not yet arbitraged. That requires the decay and crowding analysis and the early kill gates that Plan A runs, not the model sophistication that Plan B emphasizes. Plan A also sequences correctly for this firm. Days 1–3 kill the idea if it is already commodity or if the fundamental prior is too pessimistic (arbitraged to a t under 2, prior decay to one-third the published coefficient). This is entropy-reducing: if the idea fails before you touch code, you have not wasted build time. Plan B has a similar logic (develop/select/validate splits, walk-forward), but it embeds the crucial kill test (crowding, whether the idea is even tradeable) inside a ten-week project, not before it. Plan A will know by day 10 whether the near-term historical signal works, and by day 14 whether it is worth scaling. If it fails, the negative memo names residual hypotheses (likely audio channel, tone beyond text). If it passes, days 11–14 assess infrastructure and capacity—practical gates for a systematic firm. Plan B will know by week eight or nine whether the model is any good and whether the signal survives. Both are reasonable research timelines, but Plan A's rhythm matches the firm. Neither plan invents economics aggressively, but Plan A is more disciplined: it commits to a round-trip cost of 20bp, calculates net alpha, asks for an IR of 0.4, and then checks whether capacity exists. It does not assert a P&L; it calculates one from the post-cost returns. Plan B is more cautious on paper (it names break-even cost as a primary result, acknowledges 'possible zero'), but it also proposes a more complex pipeline and therefore has more room for ex-post selection. The ablation list in Plan B is long (LM/FinBERT/domain-adapted-DeBERTa/+Q&A-separation/+speaker-tags/+peer-relativization/+orthogonalization), and the note that Harvey-Liu-Zhu t>3.0 is required suggests the team recognizes the multiple-testing problem. But that recognition is not the same as solving it through pre-registration; Plan B's pre-registration is in a dated git commit (good), but the ablation runs are explicitly scheduled post-validation split (confusing and opens a tree of researcher degrees of freedom). Plan A's pre-registration is frozen on day three and explicitly gated: exploratory work after that point is outside the primary specification. This matters in a systematic firm because the research committee will re-run the code, and a plan that cannot tell the chair whether a variant was primary or exploratory will not move money. Both plans address the right question and use reasonable data. Plan B's data choices are slightly more careful (point-in-time GICS membership, explicit delisting codes, Markit borrow, Corwin-Schultz spreads), but Plan A's are sufficient and materially simpler to implement (no Snowflake, no gold annotation loop). Plan A has a real weakness: it does not separate CEO and CFO tone, does not model hedging language or answer evasion, and uses a standard word list (Loughran-McDonald) rather than a fine-tuned model. If tone in the CFO's Q&A answers is fundamentally different from tone in prepared remarks or management's opening statements, or if hedging language is the true signal and standard tone misses it, Plan A could fail to find an effect that Plan B would catch. The appendix in Plan A lists these as pitfalls and proposes boilerplate language and LLM lookback as the residual hypothesis after failure. Plan B would know this by week four. So the risk is: Plan A might kill the idea too early, not because the idea is dead but because the simplest measurement misses the signal. Against this, the evidence in the literature (Price-Doran et al., Mayew-Venkatachalam on vocal affect) suggests tone is robust to measurement choice; Bochkay-Hales-Sengupta finds effects in CEO-only tone; and if the signal were so fragile that only a fine-tuned model would find it, it is probably too weak to trade. Plan A's gate of a t of 2.5 clustered is defensible given the decay prior and the cost of false positives; Plan B's t of 3.0 is higher. But for a systematic firm in 2025, an effect that needs a BERT model to emerge is a bad trade: it is code risk, it will decay faster as the finding becomes known, and it is hard to explain to a risk manager. Plan B's model-separation work (whether the effect is in the Q&A, whether CEO and CFO differ, whether evasion matters) would be valuable *after* Plan A establishes that a simple tone effect survives. That is a sequential decision: first check whether there is a signal at all (Plan A), then decompose it if it is real. Plan B does both simultaneously, which is thorough but risks sinking cost before establishing whether the basic hypothesis works. One other issue: Plan B's statement that the 'encoder is never fine-tuned on returns' is good practice but also means the tone model is not optimized for predicting what matters. In a systematic firm context, that is backwards. You want to optimize for predicting next-quarter peer-relative returns, not for matching annotation. The walk-forward structure somewhat repairs this (the model sees 2015–2020 transcripts during training, then predicts 2021–2022), but the core objective remains off the task. Plan A uses the final 63-day return as the outcome and works backward from that; the tone measure is chosen because prior research and economic logic suggest it should matter, not because a model says so. This is less sophisticated but more defensible. Plan B's answer is that the gold annotation ensures the model measures tone correctly, and the final regression of the signal on returns controls for the offset. This is reasonable, but it adds an extra layer of potential misspecification: if the model measures tone well but tone does not actually predict returns, the sophistication does not save it, and if tone predicts returns through a channel the model does not capture (e.g., vocal stress, pause length), it will miss it. Conviction: Plan A is the clearer choice. It matches the firm, the timeline, the decision gate, and the error asymmetry. It is built for a question about a tradeable signal in a systematic context, not a question about whether a phenomenon is real. The main risk is early kill due to an oversimplified measurement, but that risk is acceptable given the prior evidence and the cost of committing a month to a more complex pipeline. Plan A will know in two weeks whether the idea is worth pursuing, which is the right rhythm for a 200-quant systematic firm. Confidence is 4, not 5, because Plan B's model work is genuinely sophisticated and could find an effect Plan A misses, and there is nonzero probability that the firm's infrastructure would enable Plan B more easily than imagined (they might already have Snowflake and BERT fine-tuning pipelines in house). But the modal outcome is that Plan A produces a faster, cleaner decision, and that is worth more in this setting.

result.key_differentiator: Plan A identifies a tractable mechanism-level question and sequences to kill false positives early; Plan B conflates a single-name multiple revaluation with a cross-sectional behavioral claim that cannot be answered from its data.
result.rationale:
The research question asks whether *mechanism* drives *re-ratings* — an efficiency and persistence question, not a cross-sectional elasticity at one instant. Plan A understands this. It reframes the question into three separable claims: (1) Do revisions move enough to measure? (2) Does *sensitivity* vary across regimes in a way that would be invisible in a pooled cross-section? (3) Is the initial re-rating persistent or mean-reverting? These are mechanism questions. Plan B restates the question as 'what is the contemporaneous cross-sectional elasticity of forward multiples to CAGR revisions' — answerable, but it is not what was asked. A fundamental long/short fund sizing positions on named companies across a 6-18mo horizon needs to know whether a revised growth path will actually pull through to the multiple, or whether the market has already priced it, or whether it will overshoot and revert. That is Plan A's problem. Plan B's problem is whether the elasticity is large or small, which is useful for risk attribution but not for predicting position returns.

On firm fit, the gap is stark. Plan A is written for a fundamental shop: it uses transaction-level data that this firm routinely licenses, runs monthly cross-sectional regressions (core competency), and produces a yes/no answer on a mechanism the PM can reason about. The output — 'sensitive in high-vol regimes, underreacts over 1-12mo' — directly changes sizing. Plan B is written for a systematic factor shop: it stacks macro controls in FE, builds a replicable quintile sort, reports elasticity in basis points per 100bp revision, and uses three-stage DCF theory to validate it. The eight-way robustness grid assumes unlimited human attention to specifications. Critically, Plan B uses *contemporaneous* cross-sectional analysis (sub-industry×quarter FE, quarterly snapshots) which absorbs all within-window information and cannot distinguish revision from realization. For a fundamental shop trying to predict whether to *maintain* or *trim* a position after a revised CAGR, whether the multiple moves in the same quarter the estimate does is not the question — whether it finishes moving 6-12 months later is.

On sequencing, Plan A puts the kill gate first: does consensus move enough in this dataset to support inference at all? If ≥20bp peer-relative abnormal return per 100bp revision in the pooled announcement window fails, stop. This is cheap and removes 60% of failure modes before touching regime stability. Plan B schedules this check much later (economic validation section) and proceeds optimistically. Plan A front-loads the leakage check (reverse-window CAR and event-time causality via TAQ), which is where the true risk lives. Plan B mentions but does not isolate reverse causality from confounding and does not use intra-day data to bound it.

On error asymmetry: Plan A explicitly states it is running against Type I, which is correct for a concentrated book where a false positive (over-weighting a name or reversing a thesis on bad evidence) is expensive and non-diversifiable. Type II — missing a real effect — is capped because the fund will short or trim if the thesis fails, so downside is bounded. Plan A's gatekeeping and Benjamini-Hochberg are therefore well-placed. Plan B uses no multiple-testing correction and pools across 150 sub-industries with no stated primary hypothesis, treating false discoveries as a quantity to be managed *after* the fact. For a concentrated shop this is backwards.

On measurement validity, Plan A measures the thing that matters for a fundamental investor: peer-relative abnormal return around the announcement, which is what you can act on. It avoids forward multiples by using LTM EBITDA in the denominator (realized, not estimated), sidestepping the circularity entirely. Plan B uses NTM (estimated) EBITDA and attempts to control for it mechanistically — the identity Δlog EV=Δlog EBITDA_NTM+Δlog multiple — but this is a purely accounting constraint and does not solve the inference problem. The revision variable and the denominator remain entangled. Plan A bypasses this by not using forward multiples at all.

On horizon, Plan A's primary CAR window is (−1,+1) with event-time tests of drift out to day +252. This matches a 6-18mo fund's need to know whether the market re-rates over weeks or months and whether reversals occur. Plan B's quarterly snapshots and contemporaneous cross-section cannot distinguish timing and will wash out any underreaction or overreaction that spans multiple quarters.

Plan B has real strengths: the H3 interaction (dispersion as a moderator) is a smart mechanism test, the within-industry quintile sort out-of-sample is a practical validation a PM can trust, and the Bayes shrinkage on industry elasticities is technically sound. The controls are comprehensive. But these strengths are deployed on a different question. Plan B would be the better answer if the research question were 'what is the fair elasticity of multiples to growth revisions across industries?' — a useful risk-management question for a systematic book. It is not what was asked.

On breadth and capability, Plan A uses only infrastructure this firm has (panel study, no production ML), writes to a PM who can trace every step, and produces something defensible: 'the re-rating is unstable across regimes and underreacts systematically' has clear refutation conditions and is not a black box. Plan B's interaction and shrinkage are more sophisticated but also harder to defend — if the dispersion interaction fails to emerge (β3 near zero), Plan B has no fallback. Plan A's regime gates provide branches.

The confidence is 4, not 5, because Plan A is unusually complex for a desk this size, and one engineer cannot maintain point-in-time I/B/E/S detail files and 2-way-clustered VCE without external support. The complexity is earned — the question is hard — but it is a real constraint. Plan B is easier to execute but answers the wrong question.

result.key_differentiator: Plan A directly measures what drives peer-relative multiple re-ratings as a position-sizing input to a fundamental long/short book; Plan B deflects into regime-stability inference and efficiency testing that answer whether the market is rational, not whether the fund should size around the effect.
result.rationale: The research question is explicitly about whether growth revisions drive multiple re-ratings among peers—a position-sizing input for a $6-9B concentrated book. Plan A answers this. It estimates the elasticity (β: how many basis points of multiple per 100bp of CAGR revision) and tests it directly with controls that matter for a fundamental manager: market-cap bucketing, analyst-count staleness, within-industry dispersion separating firm-specific signal from noise. It delivers a number a PM can use: "peers with 2pp EBITDA-CAGR beats re-rate by X basis points forward multiple, coefficient is Z basis points." Plan B, by contrast, redefines the question entirely. It pivots to testing regime-dependent stability of the elasticity (does β differ when VIX is high vs low, when discount rates are moving vs stable?) and to market efficiency (does the re-rating reverse over the next 6-12 months, implying overreaction?). These are legitimate research questions. They are not *this* question. A fundamental manager asking about drivers of peer re-ratings is asking for an input to position sizing on names they have conviction about—the kind of second-order insight that makes the difference between +2% and -2% alpha on existing positions. Whether the market is in a high-beta regime or whether the initial shock reverses is useful context for position-time horizon, but it is not position-sizing information. Plan B's framing also inverts error costs. For a six-to-eighteen-month fundamental book, false negatives (missing a real multiple lever on a conviction name) cost more than false positives (being wrong about a 50bp re-rating sensitivity). Plan B's regime-stability gates and dual-check on efficiency buy conviction by discarding positive betas that come and go—which is appropriate for a systematic trader sizing across 500 names with a tight Sharpe constraint, not for a 30-person shop with $50-100M per name. Plan A assumes the elasticity exists and exists stably enough to use, then estimates it. That is the right assumption set. Plan A also sequences information better. It opens with the simplest question (does the relation hold in the raw cross-section?) and adds controls/robustness only where the simple version might fail. The placebo test (random peer reassignment should kill the signal) is early and low-cost. Plan B sequences backwards: it spends two-thirds of the budget testing whether the elasticity is regime-dependent before confirming the elasticity exists in the first place. The "first-stage threshold" (β≥20bp t>5 or stop) is framed as a gate but comes only after the regime-stability work. Plan A's technical execution is also sounder for this firm. Plan A uses two-way clustering plus Driscoll-Kraay (standard for panel studies with time-invariant and cross-sectional dependence) and acknowledges the mechanical bias from using revised EBITDA in both numerator and denominator (EV/EBITDA mechanical identity check). Plan B uses Fama-MacBeth + Newey-West, which is appropriate for daily event studies (which Plan B is not); for monthly cross-sections with six-month to annual dependence, it underestimates standard errors. Plan B's event-study design (50bp threshold for "revision," off-cycle window, TAQ reverse-causality check) is textbook for testing market efficiency but adds latency and cost a fundamental analyst does not need: they care whether consensus EBITDA moved by enough to re-rate a peer, not whether it moved on a day without earnings news. Plan B's validity for this firm is also weak on a practical level. Plan B requires: (i) hand-cleaned I/B/E/S detail files for same-analyst pairs (not available out of the box; data team would spend two weeks on this), (ii) TAQ intraday data for a reverse-causality check (the fund does not have tick data), (iii) 1,000 bootstrap replications of block-shuffled event-study samples (the engineer is one person and does not build production ML; this is near-edge territory for that staff). Plan A uses licensed consensus tape, standard Compustat/Worldscope point-in-time, reghdfe (standard in-house package), and can be run in Python or Stata in a week by one analyst. The output of Plan A—a regression table with β, controls, and robustness grids—is also the exact form a PM asking "what would have to be true for it to be wrong" expects. Answers are: "coefficients become insignificant if we control for Δlog NTM EBITDA" (shows the denominator bias), "beta is half as large in utilities as in semics" (shows mechanism is sector-specific), "leading-indicator test fails and β on t+1 CAGR is negative" (shows timing error), "placebo test collapses the signal" (shows it is not noise). Plan B's output—tables of regime-dependent Waldtest p-values and variance ratios, drift regressions, and 2SLS—does not directly answer that question. It answers "is this effect regime-dependent, and does the market efficiently price it?" Neither of those is what was asked. There are real defects in Plan A. The most serious: interaction tests (dispersion H3) and sector elasticities (H4) are likely underpowered, and the empirical-Bayes shrinkage for sector-level betas is a bit sophisticated for the audience (though it is the right thing to do). The 20pp threshold for flagging restated consensuses is mechanical and could lose real data to a single outlier. The theoretical elasticity cross-check is useful but not essential—a 2–5% empirical beta is interpretable on its own terms. And Plan A does not directly address cyclicality (does the effect hold in 2008–2009?) other than via robustness. But these are details in an otherwise well-pitched plan for the actual question. Plan B's defects are structural. It misreads what this firm asks for. A fundamental long/short manager does not need to know whether growth-revision sensitivities vary with VIX tercile; it needs to know whether a 2pp EBITDA beat lifts the forward multiple on a peer by 50bp or 150bp, and whether that is a real signal or a Zeno-cut-short artifact. Plan B builds an industrial machine for testing market efficiency across many regimes when the actual question is a second-order lever on existing conviction.
issues_with_winner: Sector-elasticity estimates (H4) may be underpowered; Spearman cutoff of 0.4 for rank stability is not pre-committed and somewhat arbitrary.
Empirical-Bayes shrinkage for sector betas is methodologically correct but may exceed the PM's comfort in understanding the output.
No explicit cyclicality test beyond robustness exclusions; 2008–2009 and 2020 should be named upfront.
The 20pp CAGR threshold for flagging restated consensuses is mechanical; a single quarter could fluke into it.
Controls include both Δlog NTM EBITDA and the multiple regression version without it, which is transparent but adds a notational/conceptual load.
Does not address whether the effect is stronger in high-multiple (growth) sectors where revisions should have larger percentage impact—may need a baseline-multiple interaction.
issues_with_loser: Redefines the research question from 'what drives re-ratings' to 'is beta stable and is re-rating efficient,' which are separate and harder questions.
Sequences validation work (stability, drift, over/underreaction) before confirming the basic relationship exists; the 'first-stage threshold' gate (β≥20bp t>5) comes too late.
Requires hand-cleaned I/B/E/S detail files for same-analyst pairs, a two-week data-team lift that should have been budgeted upfront.
Uses Fama-MacBeth + Newey-West for monthly cross-sections, which underestimates standard errors in the presence of multi-quarter dependence; two-way clustering is more appropriate here.

Event-study design (50bp threshold, off-cycle windows, TAQ reverse-causality check) is mismatched to the question; fundamental managers care about consensus EBITDA moves, not whether they leak before earnings.
Requires TAQ intraday data for reverse-causality check; firm does not have tick-data infrastructure.
Regime-stability tests (Bai-Perron, variance ratios, block bootstrap) are statistically sophisticated but do not change position sizing on a single name; they answer a different economic question.
Over/underreaction analysis via drift regressions and 2SLS adds two weeks of work and likely produces a null (drift effects are weak in the cross-section post-costs); cost-benefit is poor.
Output (stability p-values, variance ratios, drift t-stats) is not the form a PM uses to defend a position-sizing decision.

result.key_differentiator: Plan A correctly sequences the decisive filter—whether the news is already priced—before building a complex revenue model that only matters if that filter fails; Plan B inverts this, sinking analyst time into detailed bottom-up work that becomes sunk cost if the checks were already public.
result.rationale:
This is a single-name event-driven trade with a concentrated downside and a binary outcome: the catalyst either moves price or it doesn't. For a one-PM desk with no quant infrastructure and a risk manager who cuts fast, Type I error is expensive—a false long position around an earnings event in a concentrated book has naked downside. The decisive question is narrow: are the channel checks already in the price? This is answerable in days with public data, not weeks, and it kills the entire thesis if the answer is yes.

Plan A correctly treats this as a gating problem. It starts with the cheapest, fastest way to answer the most-likely-to-be-fatal question: dated broker circulation → consensus revision since that date → event-study comparison to comp moves → binary gate. If consensus has already moved 50bps on full-year revenue and the stock has captured the implied move, there is no edge and no long, regardless of whether the checks are true or guidance will rise. This gate lives in days and costs nothing; the risk manager can read it; compliance can review it. Only if the checks are notes that haven't reached consensus, or haven't moved the stock, does the second question matter: *will* management raise?

Plan B correctly identifies the second question—in-year revenue sensitivity, ramp mechanics, guidance philosophy, flow-through—but front-loads a 3-4 week deep dive into bottom-up revenue reconstruction, expert calls, Monte Carlo, and regressions before asking whether any of it matters. The work is competent; the sequences are real concerns (churn, ACV decay, multi-year contracts). But it commits analyst time to detailed models of revenue impact when the first filter—did the sell-side already do this analysis?—should eliminate the idea. The plan includes a validation step (backtest prior channel signals), which is good, but it is buried at the end. If the backtest says "positive checks 6/8 times but raises only 3/8: the signal is uninformative," that work is sunk and the desk has spent three weeks learning what Plan A would have known by day two.

Both plans correctly recognize that the default is no—the burden of proof is on the long case, consensus is biased toward the middle, and management is usually conservative on full-year raises mid-calendar. Both include appropriate gates and validation. But they differ in what they ask first and what they do with the answer.

Plan A's weaknesses:
- Event study requires careful comp selection and may be noisy on a concentrated stock; the three-gate structure is correct but the thresholds (0.5% full-year, 1 SD, 1.2x straddle) are rough rules of thumb, not derived from the stock's volatility or the check size.
- Stage two (guidance history, pass-through, RPO lag) is well-sequenced but still assumes stage one passed; if stage one kills it, this work is never built.
- The plan notes the checks are "non-random, undersized" but leans on them anyway; it doesn't pull hard enough on the question of denominator.

Plan B's weaknesses:
- Inverts the sequence. The bottom-up revenue model (reconstructing 12 quarters, fitting ramp curves, expert calls on logo delta, Monte Carlo) assumes the fundamental question is resolved; it is not.
- The backtest is correct and powerful—it directly asks whether prior channel commentary predicted guidance raises—but it should run first, not as validation at the end. If positive checks didn't cause raises 3/8 times, the entire thesis is dead regardless of how good the bottom-up model is.
- Sinks time into "alternative" data (LinkedIn headcount, G2, HG Insights) before asking whether the news is already public.
- The position rules (FY revenue ≥75bps, ≥50bps above consensus, raise ≥1.5x median) are sensible, but they are gates that belong in stage one, not stage two.
- Creates a secondary long thesis ("record the twelve-month case") that widens scope and mixes objectives; if the print is not a catalyst, the desk should be exiting, not pivoting.

For this firm and this question, Plan A matches the problem. Single-name, weeks-to-months horizon, binary outcome, concentrated downside, no in-house modeling. The plan kills bad ideas fast and only builds the expensive second stage if the first one doesn't fail. It relies on public data (broker circulation, consensus, stock moves, historical transcripts) that the desk already consumes. It produces a go/no-go decision in time for the event. And it correctly handles the fact that the checks are non-random and possibly already known: that is the first thing to test.

Plan B is not wrong; it is built for a different firm—one with longer horizon, more capacity, and a need to build an ARR thesis that outlives the print. It is also built for a different question: "Should we model the in-year revenue impact and the next-year ARR case?" That is a good question, but it is not the question being asked. The question is whether there is a long around the catalyst. Plan A answers it. Plan B answers it only after doing three weeks of work that may not matter.

Confidence is 4, not 5, because Plan A's event-study methodology is noisy and the thresholds are rough; if the desk has strong priors about the comp basket or the check size was smaller than Plan A assumes, Plan B's thorough bottom-up work could catch something Plan A's filter misses. But the burden of proof is on Plan B to show that the extra cost is worth it, and it does not make that case clearly. On a concentrated book with a risk manager who cuts, fast and cheap beats thorough and slow.
issues_with_winner: Event-study thresholds (0.5%, 1 SD, 1.2x straddle) are illustrative rules of thumb, not calibrated to this stock's realized volatility or the check's probable size; a second analyst should repull if the gate is close.

The 12-16 quarter guidance table is manageable but introduces selection bias in CFO tenure and policy changes; the plan correctly notes wide CI but does not propose confidence intervals on the base rate itself.

Comp basket selection is pre-committed (good) but six-ten comps on a micro-cap may not control for size, growth, or guidance style; the re-run with a plain market model is the right hedge but should run in parallel, not as a check.

The reverse sandbag trap (conservatism priced in) is named but the plan does not explicitly test it—e.g., by comparing guidance beat rates to sell-side positivity; a comparison of whisper to consensus on prior quarters would sharpen this.
Stage two does not fully address whether new logos sit inside NRR noise or are additive; a customer count delta from the checks should be isolated against base NRR variance over 12 quarters.
issues_with_loser: Buries the most-likely-to-be-fatal test (is it already priced?) until the end, after weeks of bottom-up work are sunk; the validation step correctly asks "did prior checks predict raises," but it should be the first filter, not a post-hoc check.

The bottom-up revenue model (ramp curve fitting, Monte Carlo) is well-intentioned but commits analyst time before establishing whether the news is fresh; if the broker circulation was weeks old and consensus has moved, all the detail is sunk.

Conflates two different theses: (a) will the print raise, and (b) should we own the twelve-month ARR story. These are different time horizons and different bets; the plan pivots to the second if the first fails, widening scope and mixing failure modes.

Expert calls (4-6) are correctly sourced as a check on logo counts, but they introduce live MNPI risk if any ex-employees or partners speak to unpublished information; the plan defers this to compliance but does not pre-commit to stopping the work if MNPI is found.

The position rules (75bps, 50bps above consensus, 1.5x median raise) are sensible gates, but they are stage-two gates embedded in a stage-one work plan; the plan should not get to stage two if stage one (is it priced?) has not been cleanly passed.

Monte Carlo and regression are defensible, but for a desk with no quant staff, the output (p10/50/90) is harder to defend in a trade meeting than a simple gate (priced or not, raises or not); the plan creates unnecessary complexity in the model to answer a yes/no question.
The "flat within two sessions post-print" stop is reactive and too loose for a concentrated book; the plan should have a hard size limit from the beginning, not defer it to position rules.

result.key_differentiator: Plan A asks the right question for an event-driven desk around a catalyst—is guidance going to move and is now the moment to be long—while Plan B asks whether the market has already priced the known channel checks, which is not the decision facing the PM.
result.rationale:
This is a single-name, time-bound catalyst play. The desk needs to know: (1) Do these channel checks credibly move the full-year number enough to trigger guidance? (2) Is that catalyst imminent and mispriced? Plan A directly answers both. It starts by quantifying the in-year revenue impact in basis points against guidance, recognizes that below ~75bps is inside the noise band and may not move management (a realistic operational constraint on this specific company and CFO), and only if that clears does it size a position. It uses the channel checks not to decide whether logos are real—the desk already believes that from expert calls—but to calibrate magnitude and ramp speed, which is the actual crux of whether the print surprises. The validation step is decisive: it backtests whether contemporaneous channel chatter has predicted prior guidance moves and finds the signal is weak (6/8 directional but only 3/8 raises), so it immediately flags that management may not cooperate. It then builds the position only on tight gates: FY revenue must be ≥75bps above midpoint AND consensus AND raise flow-through must exceed 1.5x prior median, AND capacity/cRPO checks must pass. This is ruthlessly aligned with what an event-driven desk does: it bets on catalysts, sizes them, and asks whether management will cooperate. The horizon is weeks to earnings, and the output—guided vs. actual revenue, expected stock reaction, position size—is directly actionable right now.

Plan B is intellectually rigorous but answers a different question: "How much of the good news is already in the price, and will management surprise us more?" That's a reasonable research question, but it is not what drives a single-name event decision. An event-driven PM does not care whether the market has priced 50% or 90% of the news; they care whether the guidance reaction will be *more* than the current implied move, and whether that creates an edge now. Plan B's stage-one gate—checking if consensus has already revised, if the CAR is already done—is designed to screen out ideas where the information is already public. But for a catalyst-driven desk, that is backwards. The notes went out to 1000 recipients; the PM only cares whether the April earnings call will move the stock from here. The fact that sell-side consensus revised 0.3% is not a reason to skip; the fact that the number could move 1.5% more at earnings, and the implied move doesn't price that in, is the reason to act. Plan B conflates "already known" with "already priced," and for a catalyst around a single discrete event, those come apart.

Second: Plan B's stage-two work on guidance history and base rates is sensible background but not the decisive check. A SaaS company's base rate of raising in Q2 is useful context, but the actual question is whether *this* Q2, with these new logos, at this scale, given the partner dynamics and services headcount, will move it. Plan A tackles that directly by reconstructing revenue bottom-up, stress-testing the ramp lag against expert calls and historical cohort data, and comparing the shock to management's documented flow-through behavior and macro caution. It can fail—the signal backtests weak—and it says so and shuts down. Plan B's base-rate approach treats all Q2s as similar and builds confidence from historical frequency, which is weaker evidence for a single event where the idiosyncratic facts dominate.

Third: firm fit. This desk has no quant staff and cannot build datasets. Plan A's data requirement—10-Q/K, transcripts, expert calls, sell-side lines—is exactly the material this desk already works with. Its methodology is transparent arithmetic: reconstructed revenue, cohort ramp curves fit to disclosures, Monte Carlo on inputs that came from expert calls, regression of past guide-to-actual flow-through. The PM can inspect every step. Plan B demands a 250-day estimation window, a 6-10-stock comp basket with two-factor models and CARs with standard errors, guidance-table regressions on CFO tenure dummies, and straddle-implied move calibration. Those are credible techniques, but nobody on this desk can evaluate them. The PM will be forced to trust the analyst's black box or spend weeks learning factor models, neither of which is this fund's strength. Plan A's complexity is all in the economic judgment—revenue reconstruction and ramp curves from SaaS mechanics—which this desk is built for.

Fourth: error asymmetry. An event-driven desk with a 12% downside stop is Type I dominant: if the thesis is wrong, they lose money on a concentrated bet. That favors the more demanding evidence standard. Plan A's gates are strict: the thesis only works if FY revenue is 75bps above midpoint *and* above consensus *and* raise is 1.5x prior median *and* the cRPO/capacity checks don't flake. It also requires validation: the signal has to have predicted raises in the past, not just been directionally correct. It finds that bar is not met (raises only 3/8 times despite positive commentary 6/8), and it is honest about that being a red flag. Plan B's stage-one gates are more modest: if consensus has revised >0.5% and the CAR is less than 1 SD, move to stage two. That is a lower bar, and the decision rule at the end ("three of four outcome states are bad, hence the default is no") is more permissive—it acknowledges uncertainty but doesn't pre-commit a threshold for position sizing. For a concentrated bet, Plan A's stricter sequencing is more appropriate.

Fifth: sequencing and adaptivity. Plan A puts the kill criterion first: backtest whether channel chatter predicted guidance moves on the prior 8 quarters, and if it did not, stop. That is entropy-reducing—it kills the thesis in a week instead of three months. If the backtest fails (as it does: 3/8), the desk learns that this signal is not reliable enough to bet on, even if this quarter feels special. The rest—building the revenue model, running Monte Carlo—only happens if that check clears. Plan B builds the full analysis always: stage one runs the event study and consensus analysis (interesting background), then stage two is done either way, then at the end it offers three pass criteria but structures them as symmetric (two of three failures kills it), which is less decisive. Plan A's flow is tighter: kill criterion, then conditional model build, then position gates.

Sixth: what a PM can actually act on. Plan A produces a number: implied FY revenue in bps vs. guidance, expected move via historical flow-through regression, required win probability to exceed the straddle, and a position size (4% NAV given the stop). A PM can read that and say yes or no. It also says: take this position only if all the gates hit, because historically this signal has been unreliable. Plan B produces a complex report: what the market has already priced, what the base rate of raises is, what prior check episodes did, confidence intervals on guidance policy. That is valuable research, but it does not close on a decision. The PM is left saying "so do we do it or not?" and the answer is "only if you believe management will surprise, and here is the base rate, but the base rate has a wide interval." For a time-bounded catalyst, that is not enough.

Seventh: the specific hypothesis. Plan A's hypothesis is crisp and falsifiable: incremental new logos add <75bps in-year, so the catalyst is not the print but next-year ARR, so the long thesis rests on a longer hold or a different event. That is a claim that can be checked and killed. Alternate: if ramps are faster/lands are bigger, in-year sensitivity is >75bps, and the print *is* live. Plan B's hypothesis has two parts both required to be wrong for a long: (a) checks already reflected in consensus, AND (b) management won't raise anyway. Both must fail to win. That is a wider hypothesis set, which makes it harder to falsify decisively and gives more ways to rationalize a miss.

Eighth: cost and timeline. Plan A takes weeks: 12 quarterly filings and 3 years of transcripts are already public; expert calls can be lined up in days; the revenue reconstruction and Monte Carlo are a few days of analyst work; the backtest on prior quarters is one week and kills or keeps. Total: two weeks, mostly parallel. Plan B also takes two weeks for the event-study and consensus work, but it's sequential: wait for the information date to be established, pull the revision history, run the event study, then build the guidance table, then compare. If the event-study window is already closed, the analysis has to make assumptions about when the checks "priced in." Both are reasonable timelines for a catalyst, but Plan A's output is faster to a decision.

Ninth: explicit kill criteria and disconfirmation. Plan A says: stop if the backtest on 8 prior quarters shows the signal is uninformative (it finds 6/8 directional but 3/8 raises—that is uninformative). It also lists the specific stops: cRPO deceleration, flat customer adds, raise at/below flow-through, falling land value, 8% price stop, flat stock within two days post-print. Those are concrete. It also names the alternate story: management might not raise because of CFO caution, macro concerns, or structural changes in recognition (prepaid contracts, ASC 606 lumpy licenses). Plan B lists pitfalls but then says "the default is no"—that is conservative, but it's not as sharp as Plan A's specific kill gates.

What is Plan A missing? The validation backtest comes back negative (raises only 3/8 times despite positive commentary), and Plan A says "stop" at that point. That is correct given the desk's error asymmetry, but it also means the analysis may kill a real opportunity if this quarter is actually different. An argument for Plan B is that it does not pre-screen based on signal reliability; it asks whether the market has already moved, and if not, builds a model for the single instance. If this quarter has faster ramps or larger lands, and the desk has good color from experts, Plan B's stage-two guidance analysis might still offer value. However, for a concentrated bet with an 8% hard stop, the desk should not be running on signal properties that have been unreliable in the past. Plan A is right to be skeptical.

What is Plan B missing? It does not directly model the in-year revenue impact. It backs it out by inverting the stock move via CAR and historical multiples, and it compares to "what checks can arithmetically deliver." But it does not go through the detailed SaaS mechanics—installed base plus churn plus expansion plus new-logo ramps against guidance policy—that Plan A builds. For a SaaS company, where the mechanics are stable and knowable, that mechanistic model is more powerful than an event-study CAR. Plan B also structures the gates as symmetric (two of three fails = stop), whereas Plan A is asymmetric and demanding (all gates must pass), which is right for Type I.

One more consideration: the actual decision is time-bound. Earnings are in a few weeks. Plan A says: can we know in one week whether this signal is historically reliable? If yes, move to modeling. Plan B says: wait for the information date and the revision history to settle, then run the event study, then check guidance history. By the time Plan B concludes, it may be the week before earnings, and the decision window is closed. Plan A is designed to produce a go/no-go answer faster, which is what a catalyst desk needs.

Conclusion: Plan A is the right frame for this desk, this question, and this horizon. It directly answers whether the catalyst moves guidance, prices the risk appropriately, and puts the decision bar in the right place. It starts with the kill criterion (does the signal work historically?), which is both efficient and matches the desk's error profile. Plan B is intellectually sound but misses the nature of the decision. An event-driven PM does not care whether the news is already known; they care whether the guidance surprise—net of already-implied move—offers an edge at the print. Plan A tackles that. Plan B does not, and instead produces good background research that does not close on the question.
issues_with_winner: The backtest result (raises only 3/8 times despite positive commentary) is a real red flag and could kill the entire thesis; Plan A is right to say 'stop' but that is a negative outcome, not a win. If this quarter is actually different—faster ramps, larger lands—the desk misses it.

The position sizing relies on a regression of prior post-earnings returns against forward-estimate changes, which could be unstable or suffer from look-ahead bias if priors were guided higher after ramps accelerated; this should be explicitly tested for reverse causality.

Monte Carlo over logo delta, land value, and lag assumes those inputs are statistically independent, but they may be correlated (faster ramps may coincide with larger lands); sensitivity to correlation structure should be shown.
The 75bps threshold is a point estimate, not a confidence interval; if the model returns 70bps with wide bounds, the decision becomes ambiguous.

Revenue reconstruction back to 12 quarters is labor-intensive and subject to misclassification risk (services vs. recurring, segment-reporting changes); the 1% tie-in is tight but requires careful audit.
issues_with_loser: Plan B conflates 'already known' (checks have been published) with 'already priced' (stock and consensus have moved by the full amount); these come apart in catalyst research, and the fact that sell-side revised 0.3% does not mean the print cannot move 1.5% more.

The event-study CAR window is arbitrary (250-day estimation, -1 to +1 and 0 to +10 day events); the choice of window and comp basket can significantly affect the conclusion. Plan B names this as a check (re-run with different basket) but does not pre-commit to the basket or explain how selection bias is ruled out.

Stage-one gates are symmetric: if full-year consensus moved >0.5% OR CAR is >1 SD OR straddle is >1.2x realized move, stop. But those are all correlated measures of the same thing: how much room is left. A single composite gate would be clearer.

Plan B's stage-two guidance analysis—extracting base rates of raises by quarter and CFO—is fine context but does not directly model whether *this* quarter's new logos move *this* CFO's guide. It relies on base rates when the specific case facts may matter more.

The decision rule at the end ('three of four outcome states are bad, hence the default is no') is conservative but not quantified; it doesn't say what confidence level justifies a position, only that most outcomes are bad. For a catalyst bet, that is too permissive.
Position sizing is not addressed; Plan B produces a research conclusion ('go' or 'pass') but not a specific P&L model or risk-budget allocation. An event-driven PM still needs a number.

The plan assumes the analyses are sequential and a negative stage-one finding kills stage two; but if the desk has high conviction from experts that the logos are real, it might want stage-two work anyway to understand guidance policy, even if the market has partially priced the move. The gating is rigid.

result.key_differentiator: Plan B stops before building a signal to test whether round-lot size actually identifies retail flow; Plan A assumes retail identification and jumps to a tradeable backtest, risking three months on a premise that may be false.
result.rationale: This is a mechanism test, not a single-name KPI or blind signal fit. The research question bundles two claims — (1) does lot size predict retail flow, and (2) is that retail flow profitable to trade — but only claim (1) is fundamental. Plan B recognizes this and erects a hard stop: test claim (1) in isolation using multiple imperfect benchmarks (sub-penny signs, RLP flags, Rule 605 wholesaler data, correlation with external retail flow). Only if round lots pass five explicit gates does Phase 2 proceed to signal construction. Plan A, by contrast, assumes round lots are a valid retail proxy and jumps directly to building an imbalance signal. This is backwards for a systematic firm. In a setting where the cost of Type II error (discarding a real effect) is bounded — the signal either works across capacity or it doesn't — but Type I error is expensive (three months wasted on a false premise), entropy reduction is paramount. Plan B's ordering is adaptive: it kills the idea early with high probability if round lots do not identify retail, and costs nothing if they do. Plan A's comprehensive architecture is a virtue if the premise holds, but it is a vice if the premise fails. A systematic firm replicates research before trading and will re-run independent checks; they value early disconfirmation over completeness within a false branch. Plan B also better matches this firm's infrastructure and culture. It uses only data and venues this firm already has (TAQ, exchange feeds, CRSP, Rule 605 reports, DuckDB/Spark), it is sequenced for human oversight (intermediate gates with explicit kill criteria), and it produces outputs a research committee can actually verify: the precision and recall of each retail identifier, the bootstrap confidence intervals on lift, the correlation of round-lot imbalance with known-retail proxies. Plan A, though rigorous, buries the fundamental check (does RLOIB incremental to ALLOIB and RETOIB have predictive power?) inside a dense prediction and cost analysis. It also inherits unexamined premises: that the Lee-Ready algorithm signs lot-filtered data validly despite the confounders Plan B names, that institutional scheduler behavior is stable across the 2010-2019 period, that a fixed 100-share threshold captures retail when the SEC later moved to tiering. Plan B acknowledges these explicitly and tests them. On cost and capacity, Plan A's breakeven-spread framing is sound, but Plan B's go/no-go at after-cost Sharpe ≥1.0 and net/gross >0.40 is a more stringent and more appropriate gate for a firm that will hold this signal for weeks and faces real crowding in short-term reversal. If the mechanism test (Phase 1) fails, the firm learns that round-lot imbalance is either capturing institutional order-flow or is too coarse a marker for modern retail behavior — both valuable facts. If it passes all five gates, Phase 2 can proceed with justified confidence. Plan A cannot readily abort a false branch partway through without waste. Both plans are well-written. Plan A's sensitivity grid, factor controls, and cost modeling are thorough. Plan B's pitfalls section is more honest about structural breaks and meme-stock bias. The deciding factor is sequencing and falsifiability: Plan B's five explicit gates and kill criteria are tailored to a mechanism test, while Plan A's architecture is tailored to signal development. Plan B is not the "safer" choice — it could fail its own gates and generate a genuine negative result, which a PM might find less satisfying than a comprehensive backtest. But for a systematic firm that values reproducibility and early disconfirmation, Plan B is the correct choice. Confidence is 2 rather than 1 because Plan A's more comprehensive modeling could uncover real effects that a gate-based approach misses (e.g., if retail round-lot imbalance has a lag structure that short correlations do not capture), and because a very deep institution might prefer to absorb the risk of a false premise in order to exploit any signal that survives the full pipeline. But on the merits of the question and the firm's apparent constraints, Plan B is superior.
issues_with_winner: The five gates (especially G1 precision/lift and G3 signing accuracy) rely on imperfect ground-truth labels; if all benchmarks are systematically noisy, Plan B may spuriously reject a real effect or accept a correlated false one.

Rule 605 wholesaler data may not be comprehensive or granular enough for odd-lot vs. round-lot breakouts, forcing reliance on benchmarks that have known look-alike problems (e.g., sub-penny signs are valid only pre-half-penny compliance).
The latent-class precision/lift estimator is non-standard and will need careful exposition to the research committee; if it is opaque, conviction will suffer even if the mechanics are sound.
Hard stops on gates (e.g., lift <1.5x lower bound kills the project) may be too rigid if the true effect is real but small; a more Bayesian treatment would update confidence without an outright kill.
Does not produce a tradeable signal by the end, only validation that the mechanism exists — a PM expecting to run on research will find this incomplete, though for a systematic firm that is correct.
issues_with_loser: Assumes round-lot size is a valid retail proxy without testing the assumption upfront; if institutional order slicing and retail migration to fractional shares have eroded the signal, three months are spent building a framework around a broken premise.

The residualization strategy (controlling for ALLOIB, ODDOIB, RETOIB) does not prove that RLOIB has incremental content; it only adjusts for multicollinearity. If round lots simply correlate with venue or price tier due to institutional slicing, the residual will be spurious.

Inherits a fixed 100-share definition despite the SEC's tiered redefinition (100/40/10/1 by price tier) partway through the sample; acknowledges this in pitfalls but does not weight or prioritize the tiered re-run, risking a structural break.

Buries the question of whether the effect is liquidity provision (positive 1-day reversal) or genuine retail misprice (negative continuation); acknowledging sign flip as reinterpretation rather than failure means the plan is not fully falsifiable — any result can be fit to the story.

The cost model, though detailed, uses a single base-case k=0.5 for market-impact square-root; for a firm with $50M–$5B in capacity, impact will vary sharply by venue and size quintile, and the 5% participation cap may not bind for all strategies, making the headline alpha figure misleading.

The list of pitfalls is long and acknowledged but then mostly set aside (e.g., 'STR relabeled' is named but then 'day-t return control is non-negotiable'); this signals awareness of problems without solving them, which a research committee will probe.

Placebos (exact-100 bucket, forward-shifted signal, within-stock-day randomization) are good, but the falsification bar (|t|<2.0) is not as sharp as Plan B's explicit gates; a plan that says 'if this coefficient is not sig, we stop' is clearer than one that names multiple acceptance regions (net alpha, gross alpha, long-leg alpha).

result.key_differentiator: Plan A tests the identification premise before building a signal, pre-emptively killing the work if round lots are not a retail marker; Plan B assumes identification and optimizes signal mechanics, proceeding to expensive downstream work even if the core claim is false.
result.rationale: This firm runs systematic signals through rigorous replay before deployment. Plan B is built for a fundamental question — 'if round-lot imbalance predicts returns, is it harvestable?' — and answers it thoroughly. But the actual question is prior: 'are round lots retail at all?' That prior question determines whether any signal is worth building. Plan A sequences correctly: it bundles the two claims explicitly, tests the logically first one in isolation with hard kills, and produces an actionable output either way (a validated retail proxy or a well-documented negative result plus pointers to better identifiers). Plan B front-loads Fama-MacBeth, factor controls, and portfolio mechanics while leaving identification to residualization and correlation checks — approaches that work when you already believe the marker is meaningful, but that obscure whether it actually is. For a systematic firm, an identification failure is expensive because the deployment machinery is smooth and the committee will re-run results; a plan that allows a false marker to survive into signal-building wastes compute and commits to something untradeable. Plan A's gatekeeping — especially G1 (Rule 605 lift + latent-class precision) and G3 (signing accuracy against RLP flags) — directly tests the identification premise using multiple imperfect labels and triangulates. It kills the project early if retail concentration is low or signing is noise, both of which are highly plausible given the institutional VWAP/TWAP scheduler reality Plan A names explicitly. Plan B acknowledges round-lot confounds in its pitfalls section but then proceeds as if residualization and correlation checks are sufficient to net them out; they are not, because a signal can be orthogonal to all-lot imbalance and still be institutional noise rather than retail. Plan B's falsification rule ('if t<2.0 at every horizon') sets a low bar — a real but small retail effect survives that gate — but it fires only at the signal level, after weeks of work. Plan A's gates fire earlier. The firm's research platform will re-run B's results anyway, so B's factor control and robustness grid are not as valuable as they look; what the platform cannot easily replicate is the identification triangulation A does upfront. Plan A is also better sequenced for adaptive work: it names what kills the hypothesis (Gates 1–5 all failing in all partitions), defines branches (Phase 2 conditional on all gates passing), and specifies that a negative result is a deliverable. Plan B schedules every stage — splits, controls, robustness, placebo — regardless of intermediate results. For a Type II dominant setting with breadth (many names, low individual signal strength, capped downside from short-squeezability), an early kill is more valuable than an elaborate confirmation. Plan B's concern about costs dominating (stated in pitfalls) is not answered by its own design; it reports net alpha thresholds and breakeven costs, but the identification question — whether RLOIB is even retail — remains unresolved. If the answer is no, the cost analysis is vacuous. Both plans show technical depth appropriate to the firm. Plan B is more complete as a deployed signal; Plan A is better for a research committee that needs to know whether the premise holds before committing capacity. In this firm's context, the prior question is the binding one.
issues_with_winner: The Rule 605 wholesaler report (Benchmark C) is described as 'cheap, spreadsheet-only, run first since it alone can kill the project' but the paper-and-pencil work of mapping MPID-by-bucket to round-lot imbalance across 2,000+ names is labor-intensive; the plan does not estimate the staffing or calendar cost of Benchmark C before proceeding. If it is slow, the early kill is delayed.

Benchmarks A and B (TRF z-scores and RLP flags) are marked as 'valid only pre-half-penny compliance' and 'very low recall,' respectively, creating a window where triangulation works well (pre-2015) and periods afterward where the labels are noisier. The plan sets gates in 36 months pre-half-penny but does not explicitly address whether gates should be period-specific or whether failure in post-half-penny data (where better labels are scarcer) automatically kills the hypothesis or just delays Phase 2.

Gate G5 (panel regression of forward returns on Benchmark A + round-lot imbalance, t>3) is a product of two noisy labels (Benchmark A itself has 'tens of percent sign error'), so high false-negative risk. The plan does not discuss whether the gate should use a pre-specified lower critical value or whether disagreement between G1–G4 and G5 triggers a re-design.

Mechanism tests (price elasticity, round-notional vs round-share clustering) are valuable but not binding; the plan does not specify whether these are required to pass before Phase 2 or whether they are confirmatory. Their placement in the spec suggests they run in parallel with gates, but the dependency is unclear.
issues_with_loser: Plan B does not test whether round lots are actually a retail signal before building and optimizing a trading strategy. It residualizes RLOIB on ALLOIB, ODDOIB, and RETOIB and checks correlation with RETOIB in rolling windows, but residualization is a dimensionality reduction, not an identification proof; a factor can be orthogonal to competing proxies and still be noise. The correlation check ('if rolling r<0.25, kill') is a secondary gate, not a primary one, and is described as a robustness, not a blocker.

The plan explicitly notes round-lot confounds (institutional VWAP/TWAP slicing, odd-lot frequency rising with price) in pitfalls but does not pre-specify how each is addressed. Price control via OLS is mentioned but not tested upfront; if price-bucketing reveals the effect is driven entirely by sub-$10 microcaps where odd-lot migration dominates, that kill criterion is not available until Fama-MacBeth results are in.

Identification relies partly on 'residualize RLOIB on ALLOIB, ODDOIB, log price/size, rerun regressions on raw and residual,' but ODDOIB and ALLOIB are themselves built from potentially misclassified lots; using noisy labels to filter a noisy label does not guarantee the signal is retail. The plan does not quantify the circularity.

The Fama-MacBeth specification controls for 'day-t return, momentum, size, book-to-market, turnover, Amihud illiquidity, volatility, price, round-lot share, institutional ownership' — a rich control set that reduces the risk of a mechanical effect, but it is applied downstream. If the effect is purely a mechanical artifact of order-flow imbalance (as Plan A hypothesizes), the controls may partially absorb it, making it look real in partial correlations when it is not.

Plan B's falsification criterion (t<2.0 at every horizon) accepts the hypothesis if any horizon shows t≥2.0. But institutional slicing may predict short-term reversals (day 1–2) via microstructure, while true retail directional flow might show 5-20 day continuation; a plan that treats day-1 and day-20 equally in a go/no-go decision risks accepting a mechanical artifact as real. The plan notes 'sign may differ by horizon' but does not specify a pre-committed hypothesis linking mechanism to horizon.

Costs are modeled (Corwin-Schultz spread, square-root impact, Markit fees) but applied late — in the portfolio evaluation, not in the identification check. A plan that finds a signal works in-sample but fails under base costs has already spent weeks; the true capacity-adjusted question is asked at the end, not the beginning. For a systematic firm concerned with transaction costs and capacity, this is a prioritization error.

The validation split (end-2019 for zero-commission transition, Jan–Mar 2021 as stress) is appropriate but reveals the plan's backward-looking structure: it optimizes a signal ex-ante on 2015–2019, then tests on a 2020-2021 holdout. If the 2021 'stress' (retail surge, memestocks, squeeze risk) breaks the signal or reveals the short-leg is unharvestable, the optimization is already sunk. Plan A kills earlier.

The plan does not state a pre-specified stopping point if identification fails. If rolling correlation with RETOIB is <0.25 in post-2020 data, is Phase 2 canceled, or are the thresholds re-optimized? The adaptive conditionality is stated in concept but not operationalized.

result.key_differentiator: Plan A retrofits a single-name narrative into the shape of a systematic signal; Plan B answers what this firm actually needs to know to avoid being wrong about the business.
result.rationale:
This is a concentrated long-only manager with three to five year holds and two analysts. The research question is not 'does the market already price durability correctly' or 'what is the economic value of committed revenue' — both answers belong downstream, in a valuation. The question is: 'will these LTAs actually hold, or will customers renegotiate them into spot pricing when supply normalizes?'

That is a mechanism question, not a KPI question. It sits upstream of any financial model. If LTAs reliably break in price, then the guided durability is false and the current multiple is unjustified; if they hold, then EV may be cheap. The firm needs to know which world they are in before they size the position. A five-person shop cannot make a three-year bet on a misunderstood mechanism — they have too little capital to absorb being wrong about the business, and rebalancing is visible and costly.

Plan A is a quantitative valuation model. It is beautiful as such: it walks from raw disclosure (RPO, backlog, LTA announcements) through a tiered commitment register, marks each dollar by strength of claim, builds a forward revenue bridge, applies historical haircuts from prior shortage cycles, and delivers a DCF-checkable answer about whether EV is justified. The problem is that it *assumes the mechanism* — it assumes that tier scoring based on contract language will predict real conversion, that enforcement risk can be haircut, that disruption from renegotiation is a secondary margin effect on a baseline of honoring. It then asks 'how much is this worth if it holds?' rather than 'will it hold?'

For a concentrated manager, that is backwards. Plan A's threshold of ≥60% revenue in Tier 1/2 is a gate on contract strength, not on whether contracts matter. A manager in this position has to establish first whether they are looking at a revenue-floor story or a cycle-peak story; only then should they price it. Plan A will produce a defensible model, but it will produce a sophisticated answer to the wrong question — it will say either 'this is worth 2x current EV if commitments hold' or 'it is worth baseline valuation if they break,' without distinguishing which world this company actually inhabits.

Plan B is a falsification framework. It does not ask 'how much,' it asks 'in what cases do these stick and in what cases do they not.' It builds a control group (20–30 prior shortage episodes across industries, split by mechanism: qualification moat vs. commodity, take-or-pay damages vs. index reopeners, prepaid vs. credit-financed) and asks what distinguished Hemlock/Wacker from container shipping, Titanium/aero forgings from MLCC. It then pre-commits falsifiers on the live case (contract-liability direction, RPO threshold, shipment tracking, obligation-table increase) that can be checked in 12 months. The output is a probability-weighted haircut, *not* a valuation — it is 'this looks 70% like the MLCC case and 30% like aerospace, so apply these odds to your base case.'

That is what this firm needs. It does not need a full DCF conditioned on assumption C; it needs to know whether assumption C is even plausible given what happened last time in similar markets. Plan B answers 'will they hold or break?'; Plan A answers 'if they hold, what is it worth?' For a concentrated manager sized for business risk, the former is binding and the latter is decorative.

On firm fit: Plan A is built for a systematic, cross-sectional researcher with access to a database, an infrastructure to maintain ratcheting historical haircuts, and comfort producing a model no single analyst can fully verify in Excel. It embeds backward induction of market-implied duration and expects real-time capacity ledger maintenance. A two-analyst shop would need to staff this every quarter and update prior-cycle haircuts as new cycles resolve. Plan B is built for a concentrated fundamental manager: read the contracts, read the transcripts, find the nearest historical parallel, apply the base rate, and wait for the 12-month falsifier checks. One analyst can do it in six weeks. A PM can defend it: 'Here are three prior cases where this type of LTA broke in price within two years. Here is what this case has in common with them. Here is what would prove me wrong and I will check quarterly.'

On error asymmetry: this manager cannot diversify away a false positive. They will own this position concentrated for three to five years. If the LTAs break on normalization and they sized it as a durability story, they will be wrong about the business, not just underperforming by a multiple. Type I error dominates — a false conviction that shortages support multiple expansion is catastrophic. Plan A's failure mode is subtle: it builds a model that works inside its assumptions (contract language predicts commitment quality) and is therefore internally impressive, but those assumptions are untested. It will produce a 'go' signal for a thesis without having first asked 'do these things actually hold in practice.' Plan B's failure mode is conservative: it says 'this looks like MLCC (breaks), not aero (holds),' and the manager passes, and it turns out to be aero. That is a miss, not a disaster. For this setting, type-II conservatism is the right error to make.

On sequencing and falsification: Plan B front-loads the question that matters — the mechanism — and defers the valuation. It names three to five specific checks that could prove it wrong within 12 months (contract-liability balance sheet spike, RPO trajectory, customs shipments, customer obligation-table growth) and pre-commits to them. Plan A produces a complex output and never says what would make it abandon the thesis. If the model comes back showing 'durability justified at 10% higher valuation,' a PM has no check on whether that confidence is earned; they are trusting the rigor of the modeling, not the validity of the premise.

On evidence standard: this is a setting where significance testing is not available. There is one company, one cycle, live. What is available is historical base rate (how often did shortage-era LTAs hold in similar markets?) and mechanism coherence (do the customer, supplier, and shipment disclosures cohere or contradict?). Plan B explicitly harvests the base rate — 20–30 episodes, split by mechanism. Plan A does not; it references 'prior semiconductor cycle' as a scalar and applies one haircut family. The firm cannot run cross-sectional regressions and should not try; they need to say 'this looks like X% chance of outcome A and Y% chance of outcome B based on history, and here is what I will know in Q3 that updates those odds.' Plan B structures that; Plan A does not.

On simplicity and sequencing: Plan B is actually simpler. It says: (1) does this company fit the 'durable' or 'cycle peak' bucket based on its contract features and industry peers; (2) what do historical analogs predict; (3) what would prove you wrong; (4) wait and check. Plan A says: (1) extract all disclosures; (2) score each dollar by tier; (3) build a segmented revenue bridge; (4) backtest on four prior shortage episodes; (5) compute haircut-adjusted EV and reverse-DCF the implied horizon; (6) compare to market. Step 5–6 in Plan A are not prerequisites for step 1–3 in Plan B. Plan B's decisive test is first; Plan A's is buried under a valuation architecture.

On execution for this firm: Plan B asks for transcripts, 10-K contracts exhibits, and a historical case library. The analyst reads, codes (take-or-pay vs. reservation, prepaid vs. credit, requalification lag), and ranks by feature. That is work, but it is the work of reading and judgment, not modeling and infrastructure. Plan A asks for the same disclosures but then requires maintaining a quarterly backlog-to-revenue conversion rate, updating prior-cycle haircuts as quarters resolve, and running a forward revenue bridge with an 8-quarter tail. That is not a three-week project; it is a quarterly maintenance burden that will drift if the analyst leaves. For a two-analyst shop, Plan A is over-staffed; for Plan B, one analyst is enough.

Issues with Plan A: (1) It assumes that contract language predicts outcome, when the operative variable is likely industry requalification lag and switching cost, which it captures only indirectly. (2) It builds a complex model (tiered haircuts, conversion rates from prior cycles, segmented revenue bridges) before testing the premise that customers actually honor these in price — the model is technically sound but conditionally naive. (3) It embeds backward-induction of market-implied horizon without justifying why the market is not already thinking this way; if shortages predict durability, shouldn't that already be in multiples? (4) The backlog-to-revenue validation uses only four prior episodes; the manager will need to decide what conversion rate to apply, and Plan A has not established whether that rate is robust or sample-specific. (5) It defers the falsification check ('if negative gross bookings two straight quarters, negative') to the end, where by then the analyst will have spent weeks building the model. (6) The output is a valuation that conditions on assumption C, not a probability-weighted assertion about whether assumption C is true.

Issues with Plan B: (1) It does not produce a point estimate of EV or quantified upside — the manager will need to combine this framework with their own valuation to size. (2) It relies on analogs (prior shortage cycles) that are imperfect — HBM is not polysilicon, auto semis are not containers. (3) The pre-registered falsifiers (contract-liability direction, RPO threshold, customs data) may move slowly or remain ambiguous; the manager may not get a clear signal even 12 months in. (4) It does not formally model the sensitivity of outcome to contract terms, so a PM might overweight or underweight the take-or-pay percentage. (5) It is conservative: it is likely to output a lower durability probability than Plan A's model, because it is anchored to base rates of renegotiation rather than theoretical recovery rates from contract scoring. (6) The read-the-contracts work is not repeatable; if the analyst leaves, the firm loses the judgment calls embedded in the coding scheme.

Override: Plan A is not wrong, it is just answering a different question than the one this firm is asking. A systematic multi-name researcher or a long-only manager with a deep in-house infrastructure would use Plan A — it is the right tool for 'how much is durability worth.' But a five-person concentrated fund, where a three-year bet needs to rest on a conviction that the business itself is as described, and where the manager's edge is business judgment not modeling, should use Plan B — it is the tool for 'will the business actually work as the company claims.'

The key differentiator is that Plan B front-loads falsification and fits the firm; Plan A is technically superior but answers the wrong question for this context. Type I error dominates; conservative historical base rates are more defensible than confident forward modeling; and mechanism-first sequencing is appropriate for concentrated risk. The manager should know by month three whether this is a real durability story or a cycle-peak story, and should not size the position until they do.
