result.key_differentiator: Plan A directly tests whether shortage-era LTAs survive normalized supply by building a replicable cross-industry framework on historical episodes; Plan B prices the current company assuming LTA durability is real, then validates backward—inverting the evidential order needed for a concentrated manager to believe the claim.
result.rationale:
The research question is: do shortage-era LTAs portend durable revenue? This is a **mechanism question with cross-sectional grounding**—it asks whether a claimed durability effect actually holds empirically across settings, not whether one company is priced right. A concentrated manager holding 25-30 positions over 3-5 year horizons cannot afford to be systematically fooled about durable revenue by a category of contracts. They need to know whether the mechanism *works*, not how to model a single company assuming it does.

Plan A builds the judgment backward from evidence. It names the specific mechanism by which LTAs survive or fail (switching cost and requalification lag, not contract language), identifies 20-30 historical episodes where that claim can be tested, and pre-commits what would falsify it (price staying above spot for 8+ quarters in low-switching-cost settings). It holds out the 2021-2024 auto-semi cycle to test predictions before accepting the framework. For the live HBM case, it pre-registers falsifiable checks checkable within 12 months. Validation is ordered right: crude checks first (does the ordering by switching cost predict outcomes better than by label?), then toward the live case. The framework is built so that a hand can spot-check 3-4 historical episodes and verify the logic; an investment committee can understand "requalification impossible = price holds, requalification cheap = price reprices" without statistics.

Plan B inverts the evidential order. It starts by building a valuation model that assumes the LTA-to-RPO gap is durable, then backtest-validates against historical episodes to "isolate what distinguished durable cases." This is backward. Backtest validation of a pricing model does not establish whether the underlying claim (LTAs survive normalized supply) is true—it establishes whether past pricing models that got the LTA durability question right also happened to get other things right. It confuses "does this valuation framework coherently price a durable-LTA world" with "are LTAs actually durable." Plan B would be excellent if the question were "given that we believe LTAs are durable, how should we model this company"; it is the wrong plan for "are shortage-era LTAs actually durable."

Secondly, Plan B imposes a **firm-fit problem**. It requires: building a quarterly forward-revenue bridge 8 quarters out, tagging revenue by strength of claim, computing haircuts across six attributes, building a tiered model with three resolution scenarios and depreciation schedules, coherence checks across DSO and inventory, and a reverse DCF for market-implied durable horizon. A five-person shop with no database, no engineers, and nobody trained to maintain models is not going to execute this or defend it to a skeptical IC. When that shop discovers the answer—and it should discover it early—it will be from a framework it understands, not from defending the internals of a multi-stage haircut model. Plan A produces something a single analyst can build and test; Plan B will either stall halfway through execution or produce a result the IC cannot inspect.

Thirdly, Plan A is **sequenced for information**. The first step is definitional: when did companies start claiming shortage-driven LTAs? This is cheap and anchors the problem. The next step is mechanism: what features predicted durability historically? This is still cheap—pull contracts, see what was different in LNG vs. containers. Only after mechanism is clear does Plan A go to the live case with pre-registered checks. This is entropy reduction: the thing most likely to kill the thesis ("LTAs reprice to spot once overhang lands") is tested first and explicitly. Plan B runs everything in parallel—it builds the valuation model, backtest-validates it, checks coherence, measures against thresholds—which means if the core claim fails, the analyst has already sunk weeks into tier-haircutting and DSO reconciliation that did not need to happen.

Fourth, Plan A directly addresses **error asymmetry**. A concentrated manager has **Type I dominant** loss: they hold the position, they believe the LTA story, and if that story is wrong they lose money on a bet sized for a 5-year hold. They cannot diversify a false positive on "LTAs are durable" away across 25 positions—the positions that believed it are all wrong in the same direction at the same time. This means the manager needs the more demanding burden of proof: show me episodes where this failed, show me why your case is different, pre-commit what would falsify it. Plan A meets that burden. Plan B's thresholds (≥60% NTM in Tier 1/2, ≥40% year-two coverage, etc.) are reasonable as gates but they are gates on *modeling*, not on *whether the claim is true*. If the claim is false—if customers renegotiate everything once supply normalizes—no tier-haircut grid will save the position.

Fifth, Plan A **tests the other side**. It explicitly names what the evidence would look like if LTAs were not durable (price repricing to spot in low-switching-cost industries), and it builds the framework so that a negative case is as visible as a positive one. It will become obvious to the analyst while reading through polysilicon and containers whether the switching-cost story holds. Plan B does not have a clear falsifier—negative implied gross bookings and channel inventory signals are useful but they describe a *current situation*, not a test of the mechanism. A backlog-to-RPO reconciliation tells you whether the company is disclosing consistently; it does not tell you whether the company is right about durability.

Lastly, Plan A **kills the idea early if it should die**. If the analyst works through polysilicon, auto semis, and MLCC and finds that the switching-cost predictor does not separate durable from non-durable, that is a hard signal in a week. If the mechanism fails, the current company fails, regardless of how good the model is. Plan B will take 3-4 weeks to scaffold the valuation model before discovering whether the mechanism even works.

Plan A has real issues: definitional drift is real and hard to solve; survivorship bias (failed suppliers vanish) is hard to eliminate; and the analyst will need to read some contracts and understand customs data, which takes domain work. But these are the *necessary* difficulties of the question. Plan B's issues are that it answers a different question—how to price a company if LTAs are durable—and it does so with infrastructure a small fundamental shop cannot maintain.

result.key_differentiator: Plan A answers the actual question — whether this specific licence renegotiation poses a near-term margin risk — while Plan B builds a cross-sectional predictive signal that may never resolve the question for this company.
result.rationale:
This is a single-name fundamental question about one transaction with a near-term decision deadline. The portfolio manager needs to know whether *this* vendor licence renegotiation, for *this* company, materially threatens margins before guidance, not whether management evasiveness generally predicts margin surprises across a broad panel.

Plan A directly sizes the licence, maps the contract mechanics, reconstructs the vendor's pricing behavior toward comparable customers, and stress-tests margin impact across realistic scenarios. It produces a defensible answer to the specific question in weeks: margin hit of 30–90bps (immaterial) or several hundred basis points (material) depending on whether this is a routine renewal or a metric-change step-function. A five-person concentrated fund can act on this immediately.

Plan B builds infrastructure to detect predictive content in management evasiveness across ~40,000 firm-quarters. Even if it works — and there is real signal here, and the methodology is rigorous — it answers a different question. It will tell you whether deflection predicts surprises *in aggregate*, calibrated over 15+ years of panel data, producing a cross-sectional factor. For *this company's* *imminent* licence negotiation, it cannot land faster than Plan A, will carry validation overhead Plan A does not need, and leaves the actual margin number unquantified. The PM still has to do the fundamental work Plan A automates.

For a concentrated long-only fund, being wrong about the business is the failure mode, not crowding or signal decay. Plan A confronts the business risk head-on. Plan B treats the question as a testing ground for a general prediction method, which is appropriate for a systematic multi-name book but misses this firm's actual constraint: two analysts covering 25–30 names who need to know whether to flag this position for repricing or hold.

The firm cannot operate the infrastructure Plan B requires. No data scientists, no database, no ability to maintain and validate a five-family NLP pipeline across 15 years of transcripts or to re-run falsification tests if StreetEvents or Refinitiv changes a transcript. Plan B is written for a 50-person quant team at a $10B+ systematic fund with a dedicated infrastructure and research platform. When it lands, the team at this firm will not be able to independently verify the classifier's calibration, audit the hand-labels, or defend the embedding model to an investment committee. "We bought a signal that is significantly out-of-sample, but we cannot show you how it works" is not how this shop operates.

Plan A's execution is also more adaptive. Step 1 either shows the licence is 0.5% of opex (kills the investigation) or reveals it is 3–5% (opens Step 2). A 5% spend is not a risk; a 5% spend with a metric-change clause in a high-switching-cost market is. The investigator can stop early if the contract protects against uplift, or if the prior two renewals were benign. Plan B's entire statistical machinery is a prerequisite; nothing can be dropped based on intermediate findings.

The tonal evidence is handled correctly only in Plan A. Yes, tone in a live negotiation is confounded by the negotiation itself. Plan A dismisses it explicitly and substitutes a mechanical argument from contract mechanics and vendor behavior. Plan B builds an entire empirical scaffolding around the tone signal, calibrating it within-speaker and within-firm, validating it out-of-sample, and still ends up with a probabilistic prediction, not a margin number. That is mathematically defensible but answers a weaker question: "Is the signal present?" rather than "What does it cost?"

Error asymmetry favors Plan A decisively. Concentrated books have explicit loss and asymmetric downside. A false positive — deciding the licence is a major risk when it is not, and selling or downgrading unnecessarily — is a real miss. A false negative — missing a material margin shock — is also costly, but the concentrated manager has already accepted the risk by holding the position, and true negatives are costless (they hold and are vindicated). Plan A's approach — size the spend, map the contract, calibrate the distribution, back-test against history — imposes a demanding burden of proof appropriate to this error asymmetry. Plan B's cross-sectional factor, by contrast, is built for false-negative penalty: it casts a broad net to catch real signals across many names, accepting false positives as a cost of breadth. The two plans have opposing risk appetites, and the concentrated fund's risk appetite demands Plan A.

Plan A also respects the time horizon. A vendor licence renegotiation lives on a calendar: renewal date, term length, phasing schedule. The question is whether margins are materially at risk *in the next quarter or two*, not whether evasiveness predicts surprises *one to four quarters out* on a panel average. Plan A delivers confidence in weeks; Plan B will take months to execute, and even then produces a cross-sectional estimate that may not resolve the specific timing for this company.

Plan B is not poorly executed — the methodology is sophisticated, the validation is thorough, and the pitfalls section is honest. It is the wrong tool for the job. It is a building-a-signal project dressed as a single-name risk question. The fact that you cannot run it here is secondary to the fact that it does not resolve what you need to know.

result.rationale: This is a concentrated long-only manager with $400M AUM, five people, no infrastructure, and no ability to maintain the machinery Plan A proposes. More fundamentally, the question is not 'does evasiveness on earnings calls predict margin surprises broadly' — that is an interesting research project but not what was asked. The question is 'is this vendor risk material and what should we expect on the next quarter's results.' Plan A treats this as a category-building exercise: developing a cross-sectional signal on evasiveness predicting margins across ~40,000 firm-quarters. Even if executed perfectly, it answers a different question. A manager considering a concentrated position wants to know the dollar and percentage margin exposure to this one negotiation right now. Plan B starts there: it sizes the spend, structures the contract terms, estimates what the vendor is likely demanding, compares to history, and produces a sensitivity table that lets a PM decide whether the observed caution is warranted or a warning sign. Plan A requires hiring infrastructure this firm cannot support (transcript licensing, NLP pipeline, embedding models, data curation, statistical validation against a panel no one here knows how to evaluate). The output — 'evasiveness predicts margins at t|t+2 with t=2.5' — is useless to an IC that cannot inspect the evasiveness measure and does not care whether the effect works for GE or Adobe. Plan B is executable by one analyst in four weeks: pull the 10-K, build a DCF/sensitivity table, talk to industry contacts, back-test against last renewal, report the margin-at-risk in basis points and the factors that would change the call. A PM can defend 'the licence is ~2% of COGS, bad case is 20% uplift phased over three years = 60bps margin hit, we've seen 15% uplift on the last renewal' to an IC. The evasiveness observation becomes a piece of a story, not the story. Plan A's error here is not technical — the pre-registration, the source-robustness check, the reverse-causality control are all sound. The error is that it solves the wrong problem at enormous cost. For this firm, small N, concentrated, business-fundamental risk dominates, Type I error (being wrong about contract mechanics) is the killer. Plan B is built for Type I dominance: it closes off the most dangerous misreadings (metric changes, hidden uplifts, capitalization timing) before they cost capital. Plan A has high Type II risk (missing an effect that is real) as its primary design concern, which is backwards here. Plan B also sequences correctly: it starts with the size question ('does this matter enough to care about?'), then the mechanism, then validation. Plan A schedules evasiveness measurement first and never asks whether the margin dollars justify the attention.

Assumes analyst can access contract detail from public disclosures and can evaluate 'reasonableness' against comparable vendors; requires some subject-matter judgment; appropriate for a fundamental manager.

result.key_differentiator: Plan B gates on whether the core mechanism (panel MAU predicts seat growth) even exists before attempting to predict ARR; Plan A assumes the mechanism and jumps to ARR prediction, which answers a question that doesn't matter if the foundational claim fails.
result.rationale: This is a mechanism-testing question disguised as a nowcasting question. The research asks whether MAU predicts ARR. But that only matters if MAU genuinely measures seats — if the mechanism linking portal logins to billable seats is real. Plan A builds a sophisticated ARR prediction engine without ever establishing that its fuel (the MAU→seats link) exists. It treats MAU-to-ARR as the target and validates it on out-of-sample ARR forecasting. Plan B reverses the sequence: it gates first on the actual causal claim (does panel MAU growth = seat growth, measured against disclosed seat counts where available?), and only if that passes does it attempt ARR prediction. For a concentrated manager being wrong about the business is the kill condition. The business question here is whether portals measure utilization in a seat-based vendor. If they do not — if, say, paid seats are relatively fixed at contract renewal and MAU simply measures within-contract churn or free-tier adoption — then an ARR predictor trained on MAU will work in sample and fail in deployment. Plan A's validation (beating benchmarks on ARR forecasting) is backwards. It can show that MAU correlates with ARR while the mechanism is broken. Plan B's gate is the hard thing that kills the hypothesis early. Plan A's sophistication (panel cointegration, Westerlund tests, wild cluster bootstrap, ECM forms) is well-executed but addresses the wrong failure mode — it hedges against statistical fragility in an ARR prediction, not against whether the mechanism exists. For a firm with no data infrastructure and two analysts, Plan B's conditional branching is also more suited to them: it says explicitly what kills the idea and stops there. Plan A is a full research program on ARR prediction that requires completed infrastructure investment before discovering the premise is broken. Plan B puts the kill criterion first. Plan A's data spec is tighter and more technically ambitious; Plan B's is more adaptive (inspect>25% breaks, coverage drift thresholds). Both identify similar universes and data sources. But Plan A's insistence on >70% seat revenue disclosure and authenticated-hostname-only tracking is more stringent in ways that could be wrong — many per-seat vendors do not separately disclose seat counts (Salesforce), and authenticated hostnames sometimes undercount via SSO pooling. Plan B names this as a diagnostic check (coverage-trend warning) rather than a fatal exclude. Plan B is also more honest about what ARR variance decomposition can and cannot do. It publishes Var(ARR)=Var(seats)+Var(price)+2Cov upfront and scopes the nowcasting claim to companies where seats dominate ARR growth. Plan A sets a 3% MAPE bar without establishing whether that bar is even attainable given price/mix drift. Plan B's forecast horizon (five business days after quarter end, plus t+1) is also more realistic for a long-only manager than Plan A's implicit claim of using quarterly MAU to predict quarterly ARR — the timing assumes you will know Q3 MAU on the day of Q3 earnings, which is false. Panel vendors report with lag. Plan B specifies this (t and t+1 contemporaneous, then lagged). One criticism of Plan B: the ridge regression and empirical-Bayes shrinkage toward pooled estimates is a layer that a five-person shop will struggle to defend to an investment committee, and it is scheduled before validation. Plan A's fixed-effects specification is simpler and more transparent. But Plan B gates that on a pre-committed success criterion and produces working code sooner — if the gate fails, the shrinkage is moot. Plan A's Diebold–Mariano test on a forecasting hold-out is the right validation frame; Plan B's Clark–West is appropriate for nested models but only matters if the gate passes. The overriding issue: Plan A will produce a publishable result (an ARR predictor with good out-of-sample performance) even if the core claim (MAU=seats) is false. Plan B will either validate the mechanism or stop. For a concentrated book that can afford to be wrong about one name but not about the underlying thesis, Plan B's ordering is correct.
issues_with_winner: Ridge regression and empirical-Bayes shrinkage introduces machinery a small shop may struggle to implement and defend; should be defended as necessary, not defaulted to. Plan B does justify it (nested CV on training folds only, pooled shrinkage) but this is less transparent than Plan A's fixed-effects approach.

The gate itself (β in [0.5,1.5], within-company partial correlation ≥0.45, lead/lag diagnostics) is tight and risks false negatives if panel coverage is uneven across the sample; Plan B mitigates this with coverage-trend warnings but does not fully address whether the gate is calibrated correctly a priori or tuned post-hoc.

Plan B's validation relies on Clark–West and directional accuracy >60%, which are meaningful but less standard than Plan A's Diebold–Mariano; the bar of 15% RMSE reduction versus damped persistence is reasonable but not pre-registered, making it vulnerable to specification search.

The nowcast specification (α_i + φ·Δ₄ln(ARR)_{t−1} + β₀·g^mau_t + β₁·g^mau_{t−1} + δ·Δ₄ln(price index)_t) keeps the lagged dependent variable, which weakens the claim that MAU is the true driver; the lagged ARR growth dominates in most forecasting tasks, and the coefficient on current MAU may be mechanically small and hard to interpret.
issues_with_loser: Plan A assumes without testing that MAU-per-seat exists and moves with utilization; it controls for price drift via Wayback snapshots but does not validate the MAU→seats link before committing to ARR prediction.

The 3% MAPE bar is set without justification; Plan A does compare against consensus dispersion (a good move) but the in-sample MAPE is not a metric that controls for the fact that ARR growth is largely price/mix, not utilization.

Plan A's handling of 'shelfware' (dead product usage asymmetry via negative YoY MAU interaction) is named as a pitfall but not sequenced early; it appears in the 'Guards' section as a hypothesis-saving amendment, not as a gate. If shelfware dominates, the linear model on log levels collapses.

The sample is large (900–1,000 company-quarters across 35–60 names) but heterogeneous; Plan A's 'expect β 0.4–0.8' prior is loose, and the joint-lag specification chosen on OOS performance invites specification search despite the hold-out validation.

Plan A's falsification (refit on consumption-priced names; equal performance sinks thesis) is good, but it is proposed as a final check, not early enough to kill a doomed branch quickly. If consumption-priced vendors show similar MAU-ARR correlation (plausible, since both measure activity), Plan A will already have sunk weeks into a sophisticated ARR model.

The rolling-origin and leave-one-company-out validations are correctly proposed but are scheduled late; Plan A builds the full fixed-effects model with cointegration testing before these checks are run, so the cost of failure is high.

result.key_differentiator: Plan A gates a prerequisite mechanism (MAU=seats) before attempting economic inference, matching the concentrated firm's need to kill false premises early; Plan B treats the mechanism as intrinsic and proceeds to nowcasting, risking Type I error on a flawed foundation.
result.rationale:
The research question asks whether MAU predicts ARR, but implicitly for a concentrated long-only firm — the real decision is whether to build or hold a position. That requires first establishing what MAU *measures*. For a firm that gets killed by being wrong about a business (not transaction costs), the order matters more than the sophistication.

Plan A puts first things first: Does MAU proxy for seats at all? The gate (β positive, nonzero, bounded in [0.5,1.5], within-company correlation ≥0.45, halving without flipping, LoO stability) is brutal and appropriate. If MAU does not measure seats — if it reflects dormant users, tier mix drift, or enterprise blindness — the whole thesis fails and ARR nowcasting is worthless. This kills the bad idea early. Plan A kills it in roughly 4–6 weeks with one analyst: gate on a pooled panel, reject or proceed to ARR variance decomposition.

Plan B skips the gate. It builds a nowcasting model assuming MAU is a valid proxy (it says "MAU is not seats; the mechanism needs MAU-per-seat and price per seat drifting slowly" but then just adds interactions and price controls and proceeds). It validates on 20% holdout with three benchmarks and claims success if it beats persistence. This is methodologically sound — the Diebold–Mariano tests are correct, the rolling-origin validation is appropriate, the falsification on consumption-priced names is a check — but it never isolates whether the mechanism works. A beautiful nowcaster built on a broken MAU-to-seats link is a Type I error this firm cannot afford. Plan B's "falsification" on consumption names is a good check for scope but not for the fundamental gate: Does MAU measure seats within seat-metered companies?

For a concentrated long-only manager, Type I dominates. A false positive on a 25-stock portfolio in a 3–5 year hold generates concentrated, explicit loss. The upside is capped (outperformance is what it is); the downside is knowing-you-got-the-business-wrong. Ordering matters: in Plan A, if the gate fails, the analyst has spent 4–6 weeks and knows not to trust any nowcast built on this; in Plan B, if the underlying mechanism breaks, the analyst spent 8–10 weeks building a model that looks good on holdout but rests on sand.

Plan A also fits the firm's infrastructure. One analyst can run this: download data from Similarweb, Sensor Tower, Bloomberg, SEC filings, Wayback; merge on date; run OLS with Driscoll–Kraay SEs and block bootstrap in Stata or Python; hand-inspect the >25% breaks and coverage trends; present β̂ and two-thirds positive correlation to the IC in week 5. The gate is fully judgeable: "Does β̂ fall in [0.5,1.5] and is it nonzero at 5%?" The IC can understand it. Plan B requires more data orchestration (two panel sources, splicing on breaks, rolling-origin mechanics, multiple tests), more code maintenance, and the IC ultimately cannot inspect why the nowcaster works — they see holdout MAPE ratios and Diebold–Mariano p-values but not the underlying MAU-to-seats assumption.

Plan A has real flaws: the gate is stringent and might reject a valid signal if MAU lags seats (plan addresses this with leads/lags but it is a refinement); the variance decomposition assumes ARR = seats × price and ignores churn-reactivation noise; the 15% RMSE reduction bar is aggressive for a sparse cross-section. But these are execution details that come *after* establishing the premise.

Plan B is more thorough in breadth and sophistication — the cointegration tests, ECM form, wild cluster bootstrap, and falsification are all correct — but that sophistication serves the wrong question. It is designed to predict ARR well, not to establish that MAU measures seats. For a firm with no data scientists and an IC that thinks in narratives, adding econometric rigor to a premise never tested is costly. The MAPE validation is also easier to game: a nowcaster that beats consensus dispersion on 60% of company-quarters might be picking quarter-specific noise (earnings beats, macro surprise) orthogonal to MAU, especially if the MAU–seats link is weak and price drift dominates.

Plan A sequences correctly: gate the mechanism, then (if it passes) decompose ARR, then (if seats are the driver) build the nowcaster. Plan B sequences by sophistication instead of information: it assumes the mechanism and optimizes prediction. For this firm on this question, the first approach is the right one.
issues_with_winner: The gate is strict: β∈[0.5,1.5] and within-company r≥0.45 may reject a valid signal if MAU lags seats by one quarter or if the link varies materially by company size.
Variance decomposition of ARR into seats vs. price assumes clean separation; churn and reactivation, customer migration between tiers, and changes to the billing cycle muddy it.
Small sample: many seat-metered SaaS do not disclose seats, and those that do may have short windows; the pooled panel may end up thin in critical cohorts.

The plan does not address forward-looking validity: even if MAU→seats is contemporaneous, does that edge persist quarter-to-quarter or does the relationship decay as competitors enter or product novelty wears off?
issues_with_loser: Plan B assumes MAU measures seats without first testing the link, risking a Type I error on a false premise.

The nowcasting model (ARR on lagged ARR, MAU, price index) optimizes for prediction, not for understanding causality; a high MAPE ratio could reflect omitted confounders or MAU measuring something other than seats.
Validation on a 20% holdout is vulnerable to overfitting and period-specific noise; rolling-origin is mentioned as a robustness check but is not the primary gate.

The falsification (refit on consumption-priced names) tests scope but not the fundamental mechanism; a nowcaster that works on both consumption and seat-metered pricing suggests MAU predicts revenue growth for generic reasons, not because it measures seats.
The IC cannot easily verify the cointegration or wild bootstrap logic; the plan produces a validated MAPE ratio, but the underlying causal link is opaque.
At 35–60 names and multiple horizons with interactions, specification search is harder to control; the pre-registration helps but does not fully constrain the space.

result.key_differentiator: Plan A builds infrastructure for a question this firm cannot operate; Plan B answers the actual question—does tone predict outperformance—in a way a five-person shop can defend to its investment committee in eight weeks.
result.rationale: Plan A is a signal-discovery and calibration program disguised as answering a single research question. Its scope—building a production NLP pipeline, domain-adaptive fine-tuning, multi-stage validation across asset classes, capacity sizing, break-even analysis, infrastructure handoff—assumes a systematic firm with engineers, ML expertise, and the runway to operate a live proprietary model. This firm has two analysts and no data infrastructure. Plan A would consume 12+ weeks of someone's time before producing anything actionable, and even then it would need live model retraining, monitoring, and validation that this firm cannot maintain. Worse, it conflates two different jobs: establishing whether earnings-call tone contains genuine predictive power (answerable in weeks with simple methods) versus building a production trading signal (a months-long engineering project). The firm asked the first question. Plan A answered the second, and answered it for the wrong audience.Plan B directly answers: does tone incrementally predict peer-relative outperformance? It is designed to run in two weeks, touches the minimum viable data (transcripts, returns, earnings, guidance), and front-loads the decisive check with a pre-registered specification and clear kill thresholds. The kill criteria are mechanical and specific: t≥2.5 clustered, net spread ≥3% annualized, IR≥0.4, correct sign in 7+ of 10 years, robustness across size quartiles. These are testable. Failure is not an indictment—it is an output. A negative memo from this shop to the IC saying 'we tested it, it doesn't work, here's why, we're moving on' is what research should do.Plan A lists pitfalls but then proceeds as if most of them do not exist. Post-earnings drift 'not linear'—but the plan regresses and tests linearity nowhere early. Timestamps 'audit 200 calls'—on a 2M-call dataset. Pretraining overlap 'rerun with earlier-cutoff base'—but the cost and delay are not front-loaded; this is week-10 work if the early result is strong. Crowding 'makes break-even a primary result'—acknowledged, then buried in a vendor-search side-quest. These pitfalls are real, but naming them in a pitfalls section and proceeding with a 12-week plan is not addressing them. Plan B names pitfalls and builds them into the gate. Timestamp leakage 'worst in small illiquid names'—so measure the bottom size quintile separately, kill if it is >40% of spread. Surprise contamination—run the regression without SUE/CAR as a placebo, confirm it fails. LLM look-ahead—anything LLM is exploratory, outside the pre-registered gate, controlled for date scramble. These checks are early and cheap.The error structure here is type-I-dominant. This is a concentrated, fundamental shop. They hold positions 3–5 years. If they adopt a signal and it does not work, they lose money, not the marginal spread on a position that is 2% of a portfolio. They are right to be skeptical of models they cannot inspect. Plan A's final validation does include out-of-sample testing, Fama-MacBeth, robustness across peer definitions, and cost analysis—good design, not enough. The problem is that the process to get there is adversarial to the firm's capability and horizon. They cannot credibly maintain it, cannot modify it if it breaks, and the complexity itself is a form of hidden degrees of freedom—a 12-week all-in-one pipeline with ablations, walk-forwards, and LM retraining is an opportunity for subtle p-hacking, even if unintentional. Plan B's simpler, pre-registered, time-bounded approach is more likely to produce a result they actually believe.Sequencing is also sharply different. Plan A sequences by increasing sophistication: basic tone metrics (Loughran-McDonald), then peer-relativization, then orthogonalization, then finally the portfolio test. But this is backward. The decisive question is: 'does the effect exist at all?' That should be answered first, in a day or two, using the simplest method (LM tone on Q&A, prior-call adjusted, SUE-controlled). Only if the answer is yes does building a production model make sense. Plan B sequences correctly: pre-register in three days, test the hypothesis in 4–10 days, gate it, then decide if production infrastructure is worth building. If the kill threshold is missed, the analysis stops.Plan A proposes buying structured transcripts from S&P Global Market Intelligence (Xpressfeed/Snowflake), domain-adaptive pre-training on 2B tokens, two NLP engineers' worth of annotation work (6k gold sentences, 150k silver), GPU compute for multi-epoch training, and then expects a two-person analyst shop to evaluate and maintain it. That is not a defect in execution; it is a defect in reading the room. Plan B uses Capital IQ transcripts via WRDS (they likely have it already), applies Loughran-McDonald off-the-shelf, runs a linear regression that Excel or Stata can replicate, and commits the specification before touching the data. One analyst, two weeks, one notebook.The hedge in Plan A—'failure mode is week-eight t-stat hunting'—is present, but it is not addressed by the plan; it is only mentioned. A plan that acknowledges p-hacking and then schedules seven stages of ablations, walk-forwards, and placebo tests is not inoculated against p-hacking. Plan B addresses it by pre-registering everything and locking it three days in, turning all subsequent exploration into explicitly flagged exploratory work.Plan B also addresses the crowding question directly via vendor calls (days 1–3): if S&P Global, LSEG, RavenPack, Prattle, Amenity, etc. already sell this signal and their client count is visible, this is a commodity, and the kill criterion for a vendor-rank-correlation >0.7 is sensible. It puts that check early and makes a decision to license rather than build. Plan A mentions crowding but does not resolve it until after the six-month pipeline is built.On the actual hypothesis: Plan B tests the narrower, correct one. Does tone in management's Q&A (not prepared remarks, since those are boilerplate) predict peer-relative outperformance? Plan A tests three related hypotheses (unscripted Q&A vs. prepared, negative more than positive, baseline deviation) plus a battery of controls and robustness work. This is good science but bad sequencing. The simpler hypothesis solves the problem first. If it fails, the elaborations do not matter. If it succeeds, then refinement is warranted.Plan A's approach to validation is statistically sophisticated—pre-registration, train/select/test splits, walk-forward, Newey-West, expanding windows, deflated Sharpe, false discovery rate control—but it is designed for a 30-person research team at a quant fund, not a five-person shop. No one here will verify the code, check the merges, or debug the transcript parsing. The IC will not ask for ECE plots or reliability diagrams; they will ask: 'Did you test it out of sample? How much did it make? Is it crowded?' Plan A answers these but only after ten weeks.Plan B's validation is lighter but fit to the firm: Fama-MacBeth with Newey-West, two-way clustering (standard practice, not excessive), one pre-registered primary specification, explicit kill criteria that do not require statistics literacy to verify ('did it work in 7 of 10 years?'), and a fallback decision tree (if it works, months 3–4 are capacity and licensing; if it doesn't, we move on). That is how a fundamental shop actually learns.There is a risk in Plan B: if the effect is real but small, the t-stat of 2.5 or 2.9 (with Bonferroni) might be overly demanding. Earnings-call sentiment is unlikely to be a dominant signal; it may be a 5–10 bp effect annualized. That is within the noise of a two-week test. But this is correct triage: in a type-I-dominant setting with limited infrastructure, it is better to miss a small real effect and reject a false one than to expend three months and build a machine you cannot maintain to chase a maybe. If the effect is real and worth >10 bp, it will show at t=2.5 or higher. If it does not, the firm is not sized to exploit it anyway. Plan A's lower threshold (t>3.0 only after multiple-testing adjustment, and even then running many variants) creates a false sense of rigor. It is testing more, not more carefully.Plan B also includes one element Plan A does not: a direct check against prior work. Days 1–3 include Mayew-Venkatachalam, Larcker-Zakolyukina, and others; days 6–7 explicitly require replication in 2004–2010 with a t near 3. This is a reproducibility gate. If the effect was real in the 2000s and visible in published coefficients, it should show up again in a carefully controlled replication. If it doesn't, the signal is either genuinely arbitraged away or the original work suffered from look-ahead bias or data-snooping. Either way, the analysis is over. Plan A cites Price-Doran-Peterson-Bliss (2012) and other prior work but does not make replication a gate; it treats prior coefficients as a prior on decay rather than as a check on the method itself.One legitimate concern with Plan B: the use of transcript timestamps from Capital IQ rather than actual call start times. This introduces noise and possibly bias, particularly if timestamp recording is correlated with firm size or analyst coverage. Plan B flags this ('timestamp leakage, worst in small illiquid names') and controls by checking the bottom size quintile separately. This is less rigorous than Plan A's audit of 200 calls against EDGAR, but it is faster and sufficient for the gate. If timestamps are materially wrong, the effect will not show up anyway.Another concern: Plan B's use of Loughran-McDonald is dated. The dictionary was built in 2011; management language has evolved. Plan B handles this via the within-firm change (tone change versus prior four calls) rather than levels, which is sensible but not perfect. Plan A's domain-adaptive fine-tuning on 2B tokens of actual earnings-call language is more robust here, but only if you have the infrastructure to build it. Plan B's choice is pragmatic: start with the dictionary, see if it works, upgrade if the signal is strong enough to warrant it.Final check: is the question actually about 'single_name_kpi' or something broader? The research question is 'Does sentiment predict peer-relative outperformance?' in the portfolio sense. This is not a question about one company; it is about the predictive power of a signal across many companies. That is broader than a single-name narrative but narrower than a systemic market effect or a mechanism test. It is a 'does this signal work' question, which fits 'single_name_kpi' if interpreted as 'can we build a trading signal from this variable' versus 'does this mechanism exist broadly.' The confidence is 4, not 5, because Plan B's error rates (t thresholds, sample sizes, vendor duplication check) are adequate but not excessive, and there is some risk that a real 5–10 bp effect is missed. But the choice is clear.

Conflates two different questions: 'Does tone have predictive power?' (answerable in weeks with simple methods) and 'Can we build a production trading signal?' (months of work, ongoing maintenance). The firm asked the first; Plan A answers the second and acts as though it is the first.

Domain-adaptive fine-tuning on 2B tokens of transcript text requires either a data science hire or weeks of compute spend before the first test of the hypothesis. This cost is not justified before establishing whether the signal works at all.

Sequencing is backward: starts with simple tone metrics, then peer-relativization, then orthogonalization, then portfolio test. Should start with the portfolio test on simple tone, gate it, and only then elaborate.

Pitfalls are named but not structurally addressed. Post-earnings drift, timestamp leakage, survivorship, pretraining contamination, language drift, boilerplate recycling are all mentioned but then the plan proceeds as if they are solved by downstream checks rather than pre-empted.

Ablation study is a form of degrees of freedom: testing LM vs. FinBERT vs. domain-adapted, with/without Q&A separation, with/without speaker tags, with/without peer-relativization, with/without orthogonalization. This is a branching tree of specifications. The plan pre-registers one primary, but the ablation output will be hard for the firm to evaluate and defend to the IC without becoming statistical.

Assumes the firm will license structured transcript data (S&P Global Xpressfeed/Snowflake), which is an ongoing cost and a dependency on a vendor's parsing and timestamping. Plan B uses WRDS Capital IQ, which they likely already have.

Capacity and break-even analysis are valuable but only meaningful if the effect is real and large enough to matter. Scheduling this analysis for later makes sense; front-loading it inflates the sense of scope and cost.

The decision 'failure mode is week-eight t-stat hunting' is acknowledged but not prevented. Seven stages of robustness checks, ablations, and placebo tests create many opportunities for selective reporting, even if unintentional. Plan B prevents this by pre-registration and locking the gate in day three.

No explicit gate or decision rule. The plan does not say 'if the t-stat is below X, we stop.' It proceeds with validation, post-hoc analysis, and robustness work regardless of the intermediate result. This is scientific thoroughness in an academic context; in a busy fund with limited capacity, it is a luxury.

result.key_differentiator: Plan A answers whether sentiment predicts outperformance for a concentrated long-only manager who needs a defensible position view; Plan B answers whether a scalable, crowded sentiment signal exists globally, which is not the question and not executable here.
result.rationale:
This firm is a five-person concentrated long-only shop. It holds 25-30 positions over 3-5 year horizons and owns Excel, Bloomberg, and filings. It cannot maintain infrastructure, has no data science capability, and must defend every position to an IC skeptical of models.

Plan A directly addresses the research question: does call-sentiment predict peer-relative outperformance? It is sized for a single analyst working from existing tools. The design sequence is disciplined—pre-register the hypothesis and specification before touching data (days 1-3), run one clean specification (days 4-10), apply hard kill criteria, and only if it survives does it ask about implementation. It treats this as a yes/no question: does the effect exist, with what decay, is it crowded? The output is a binary decision on whether to add a sentiment screen to fundamental stock-picking.

Plan B was written for a systematic quant fund. It proposes:
- Fine-tuning a domain-adapted LLM on 1.5-2B tokens
- Building a multi-headed classification pipeline (tone, hedging, evasion, numeric density)
- Manual annotation of 6,000 sentences with adjudication and Krippendorff alpha
- Walk-forward retraining of the model across time windows
- A full factor-model portfolio with transaction-cost accounting, shorting infrastructure, capacity sizing, and Fama-MacBeth pooling

A five-person shop cannot execute any of this. They have no LLM infrastructure, no annotation pipeline, no engineering support, no data warehouse, and no short-selling operations. The deliverable—alpha per factor model per quintile per holding period—is not a thing this firm can inspect or act on. Assigning one analyst to build and defend a DeBERTa variant is professionally negligent.

Plan A is also better matched on firm risk. This manager is wrong about *businesses*, not about overfitting or cost. Plan A tests whether the effect survives 2004-2010 (the era of maximum mispricing before arbitrage) and measures decay post-publication. It asks directly: is this already crowded? Can we license the vendor score instead? It names a t-threshold (2.1) that kills it outright. For a concentrated book, Type I error (a false positive) is catastrophic—you buy a garbage company because the CFO sounded upbeat. Plan A's burden of proof (t ≥ 2.5 clustered) is appropriate to this asymmetry.

Plan B has a different goal: can we build a generalizable cross-sectional signal that works across thousands of names, survives retraining, handles multiple peer definitions, and produces a Sharpe ratio? That is valuable for a 500-analyst shop managing $100B. It is not the question this firm is asking. The firm wants: "If I use tone as a screen on earnings calls, will it improve my stock picks?" Plan B proposes an answer to "Can we productize call sentiment as a factor in a diversified statistical arbitrage engine?"

On evidence standards, Plan A sets a clear gate: the effect must appear with t ≥ 2.5 in the full specification, must work in 2004-2010 with t near 3 (credible pre-arbitrage), and must show a positive sign in at least 7 of 10 years excluding the March-2020 anomaly. Those are achievable, inspectable thresholds. Plan B's logic is "ablate every component and report all specifications"—useful for a quant shop, but it invites specification hunting and multiple-testing. The deflated-Sharpe and Harvey-Liu-Zhu adjustments are good, but they are controls on an inherently exploratory design.

Sequencing also matters. Plan A puts the hardest question first: does tone have an incremental effect after earnings surprise and announcement return? If no, stop. If yes, is it already crowded (vendor seats, decay)? If still yes, measure capacity and build. Plan B builds the model first (weeks 3-6) and tests afterward. A one-analyst shop cannot afford weeks of work on a feature that may not predict.

Plan A has weaknesses. LM tone is coarse, and the positive/negative split is mechanical; Mayew-Venkatachalam vocal affect is mentioned but not actually used, suggesting acoustic analysis was considered and dropped (wise for this setting, but should be explicit). The plan does not address whether CFO or CEO tone matters more, or whether tone changes in magnitude but not informativeness. The peer definition via GICS sub-industry is reasonable but not causal; firms compete across peer definitions, and TNIC is named as secondary. These are all manageable in an Excel-based robustness check.

Plan B's technical work is high quality. The annotation codebook, Krippendorff alpha, stratified sampling, and walk-forward discipline are all signs of competent experimental design. The ablation framework is thorough. But that competence is wasted on a question that is not being asked and an audience that cannot use it. A polished wrong answer is still wrong.

The tiebreaker is implementation. On day 11 of Plan A, if the effect survives, the question is: do we license RavenPack or MarketPsych, or do we code tone ourselves in Excel? That is a conversation a PM can have with one analyst. On day 42 of Plan B, if the walk-forward alpha is 25bp net after costs with an IR of 0.35, the question is: how do we productize this, staff the retraining pipeline, integrate it with short-selling, monitor decay? A five-person fundamental fund cannot answer that. The person on Plan A can say "we should buy the signal," "we should run it ourselves," or "it is crowded, kill it." The person on Plan B will have built something beautiful that nobody in the office can trust or maintain.

Confidence is 4, not 5, because both plans are competent and Plan B's technical rigor is genuinely impressive. In an abstract sense, Plan B is better science—more careful annotation, more thorough validation, more honest about failure modes. But that is not the criterion. Plan A is the better fit to the actual question, the actual firm, and the actual error asymmetry. A fundamental manager's job is not to find crowded signals; it is to identify mispriced businesses. Plan A lets one analyst answer that in three weeks. Plan B does not.

result.key_differentiator: Plan B tests whether round lots actually identify retail before building a trading signal; Plan A assumes the identification works and optimizes the trading strategy around that assumption, risking a real effect that is mechanical order-flow imbalance unrelated to retail flow.
result.rationale: This is a concentrated five-person fundamental shop with no infrastructure, no data science capability, and investment committees that demand defensibility over technical sophistication. The real question has two separable parts: (1) do round lots identify retail flow, and (2) if yes, is it tradeable. Plan A bundles these and asks whether round-lot imbalance predicts returns net of costs—a perfectly executed answer to the wrong question. If round lots are not actually a retail signal—if they are instead an institutional scheduler signature—then a profitable fade of round-lot imbalance is just a rebranded order-flow reversal, not evidence of a retail-trade-able anomaly. Plan B puts the hard question first: it designs a falsifiable test of the identification claim itself, using multiple imperfect proxies (Rule 605 wholesaler data, RLP flags, sub-penny improvement, external retail flows) to triangulate whether round-lot size genuinely predicts retail origination. This is a mechanism test, not a single-name KPI, and it demands that the mechanism be validated before the economic payoff is claimed. Plan A's sophisticated cost model, factor controls, and out-of-sample validation are all addressing the wrong premise. For a concentrated manager with one analyst and no engineering, this matters acutely: they cannot execute Plan A's infrastructure (WRDS, multiple TAQ filters, residualization, rolling-window factor builds, capacity modeling across AUM bands) without outside help or a data scientist they do not have. They *can* execute Plan B's first phase: spreadsheet-level Rule 605 data, public RLP flags, a clean partitioned analysis, and gate tests that produce a go/no-go decision in weeks rather than months. More importantly, Plan B is sequenced for information. If G1–G5 fail—if round lots do not actually correlate with retail flow at >1.5x lift, or if signing accuracy against known-side RLP executions is <60%—the entire trade idea dies, and the analyst learned this fast instead of after three months building a factor model. If round lots pass all gates, then Phase 2 becomes worth the investment. This is entropy-reducing order: kill the idea at its root if the root is rotten. Plan A assumes the root is sound and builds a mansion on top of it. Plan B's error asymmetry is also sharper. A Type I error here—concluding that round-lot imbalance predicts retail flow when it does not—commits capital to a trade based on a false premise and costs this concentrated shop real money. They cannot diversify it away; they cannot hedge it easily; and if the effect is mechanical order-flow and not retail-specific, it will likely decay or flip when the market moves. Type II error (failing to detect a real retail signal) is less costly: it just means leaving a trade on the table. Plan B's high bar (G3 signing >70%, G5 t>3, Phase 2 Sharpe ≥1.0) reflects this asymmetry correctly. Plan A's t>3.0 bar for net alpha is appropriate in magnitude, but it is applied *after* assuming the identification is correct, not *before*. Plan A has genuine strengths: the robustness grid is thoughtful, the cost model is realistic, and the pitfalls section shows real understanding of the confounds (institutional slicing, odd-lot frequency by price, RETOIB correlation). But these are strengths in the service of the wrong question. The residualization of RLOIB on ALLOIB and ODDOIB is clever, but it assumes that these other signals are exogenous and that the residual captures retail uniqueness—assumptions Plan B refuses to make without evidence. Plan B's weakness is that it cannot guarantee Phase 2 will be tractable if Phase 1 passes. RLP flags may have coverage gaps, Rule 605 data may be noisy or incomplete, and even if round lots correlate with retail flow, building a profitable signal may prove impossible. But this is not a weakness; it is honest about the risk. It also preserves optionality: the analyst emerges with a map of what identifies retail flow, which is valuable for future research even if this particular trade does not work. For a small, concentrated manager, this kind of option value is worth more than a polished signal that rests on an untested premise. The question as framed is a mechanism test, not a single-name KPI or a broad market effect. This demands that the mechanism be validated first, and that the subsequent trading strategy follow from the mechanism, not precede it. Plan B understands this; Plan A does not. Confidence is 4 rather than 5 because Plan A is not *wrong*—it is answering a related but downstream question competently, and if the identification assumption holds, the subsequent analysis is solid. But for this firm, at this moment, Plan B is the better bet.
issues_with_winner: Phase 2 is conditional and unspecified; the plan does not fully develop what happens if all gates pass, leaving uncertainty about the downstream signal design and cost modeling.
Rule 605 data and RLP flag historical coverage may be incomplete or require external licensing; the plan assumes these are cheap or available, which should be confirmed before commitment.
The distinction between meme-stock distortion and secular drift in retail behavior is real but the plan does not fully specify how to separate them (e.g., does it exclude 2021, or downweight it?).

Latent-class estimation and Hui-Walter estimators are statistical machinery that this firm's investment committee may not be able to inspect; the plan would benefit from a simpler corroborating check the committee can verify by hand.
issues_with_loser: Plan A assumes round-lot size is a retail proxy and never validates this assumption before building the trading strategy; if the identification is wrong, the entire payoff is just mechanical order-flow reversal, not evidence of a retail-trade-able anomaly.

The residualization strategy (controlling for ALLOIB, ODDOIB, RETOIB) is sound in principle but presumes these other signals are exogenous and that the residual captures retail content uniquely; Plan A does not test whether this residualization actually isolates retail flow.

The data infrastructure required (WRDS TAQ, rolling-window factor builds, Newey-West SEs, capacity modeling) exceeds the firm's technical capability; a single analyst cannot execute and defend this without external data-science help, which the firm does not have and is not mentioned as available.

The cost model, while detailed, is applied to a trading strategy whose premise (round lots = retail flow) is unvalidated; optimizing a cost model for a signal whose identification is unknown is backwards sequencing.

Validation at the split (end-2019 for zero-commission transition) is sensible, but the 2020–2021 retail surge is treated as a stress test rather than a threat to the identification assumption; if retail behavior changed structurally in that window, the earlier identification may not apply.

The plan does not pre-commit a falsification criterion for the identification claim itself; it says 'if RLOIB's incremental t<2.0, add nothing,' but this is a weak gate applied after the fact, not a hard stop on the mechanism before the signal is built.

No external check: the plan does not triangulate its retail identification against an independent data source (e.g., wholesaler Rule 605 reports or external retail-flow data) until robustness, if at all; Phase 1 validation is internal only.

result.key_differentiator: Plan A tests the premise (round lots identify retail) before building a signal; Plan B assumes the premise and builds the signal anyway, solving the wrong problem for a concentrated manager whose error cost is being wrong about the business.
result.rationale:
This firm is a five-person fundamental shop with two PMs investing $400M across 25–30 concentrated positions held years. What kills them is misidentifying which orders are actually retail. Plan A correctly identifies that the research question bundles two separable claims — (1) can round-lot size identify retail, (2) is that profitable to trade against — and insists on answering claim 1 with hard discipline before touching claim 2. Plan B skips straight to building a signal that fades round-lot imbalance, then threads the retail identification through residualization and correlation checks *after* the decision tree is already committed.

For this firm, the error asymmetry is Type I dominant. A concentrated manager cannot diversify away a false positive. Being wrong about whether round lots actually identify retail flow — and building a position around a false marker — concentrates the downside. The cost of wrongly identifying the source of order flow, then acting on it, is a blowup in a single portfolio position. By contrast, a Type II error (missing a real effect) means they simply don't get rich on this particular angle. Plan A pre-commits kill gates (G1–G5) at the front and stops before any signal is built if the identification fails. Plan B runs the full signal pipeline, computes the after-cost Sharpe, and *then* asks whether round lots added information *incremental* to all-lot imbalance — but by then weeks of analysis are sunk and the temptation to relax thresholds is real.

Plan A also fits the firm's infrastructure and skill set better. It starts with Rule 605 wholesaler reports broken by lot size, paired with FINRA OTC transparency — spreadsheet work, runnable in days, no databases or engineers required. It names a ground-truth proxy (wholesaler reports), explicitly acknowledges its limits (broken labels, recall/precision tradeoffs), and triangulates three different labels (TRF sub-penny signs, RLP flags, wholesaler bucketing). Plan B pulls NYSE Daily TAQ from WRDS, requires signing logic (Lee-Ready, tick test, EMO/CLNV), builds four separate lot-based imbalance signals, and runs rolling 250-day residualization — all defensible, but pitched at a firm that doesn't have a DBA and cannot maintain a TAQ pipeline. The operations person would not know whether the data refresh is working.

On the sequencing and design clarity: Plan A is adaptive. It says explicitly what happens if each gate fails — "kill if lift <2.0x," "kill if recall <35%," "kill if signing accuracy <70%" — and stops the work at the first failure. It produces a hard stop result (retail share estimation via latent-class methods on known-side RLP-flagged executions) that is judgeable by an investment committee: "round-lot order size predicts retail origination with X lift, capturing Y% of volume," full stop. Plan B schedules all stages in advance regardless of intermediate results. The falsification criterion comes late (Fama-MacBeth with t<2.0 on the residualized coefficient). The mechanism question (does RLOIB add information over ALLOIB and RETOIB?) is embedded inside the portfolio construction, not separated out. If the answer is "no," Plan B still has run a month of analysis and built a signal.

On defensibility to an investment committee: Plan A produces something human-auditable. The deliverable if the hypothesis fails is a breakdown of round-lot frequency by venue, venue-conditional retail identification lift, and a map of better retail markers. An IC member can follow the logic: "In lit markets with RLP flags we can identify retail with 95% precision; round lots within RLP-lit volume capture 28% of retail flow; round lots outside RLP-lit add 0.8x lift over baseline." Plan B produces a Fama-MacBeth regression, a decile sort, and a cost-adjusted Sharpe. The statement "RLOIB has incremental t-stat of 1.8 on forward returns controlling for STR" does not answer the question "are round lots retail?" It only says the signal might not be worth trading. The IC would ask: "Okay, but what share of round lots is actually retail?" and the answer would be buried in a residualization against RETOIB correlation, or missing entirely.

On invented economics: Plan B quotes "net alpha across $50M–$5B AUM" and reports a Sharpe for a notional long-short book without establishing that this firm can or would run such a book. For a concentrated long-only manager, the capacity and structure are foreign. Plan A stops short of any P&L claim and explicitly states in Phase 2 (conditional) what would be required to size: "no negative year, net/gross >0.40, in-sample Sharpe ≥1.0" — but only runs Phase 2 if Phase 1 (the identification question) actually passes. Better yet, it does not invent a position size or returns until both the identification and the signal are proven.

On the hypothesis and prior: Plan A is honest about priors. It explicitly states "H0 (my prior): round lots are uninformative once venue is controlled for" and explains the mechanism (dollar-denominated orders, fractional orders, institutional VWAP slicing into 100-share children). It then designs a test that would overturn that prior if retail has not actually migrated away from round-lot sizes. Plan B assumes round lots are a retail marker, controls for other markers, and uses residualization to isolate them — which is defensible but is backward from the true question. If round lots are not a retail marker in the first place, controlling for better retail markers will not make them useful; it will just orthogonalize noise.

Minor issues with Plan A: The latent-class method (Hui-Walter) for precision/lift estimation is technically sophisticated and may not survive explanation to an IC without a statistician in the room. However, Plan A pairs it with simpler external benchmarks (TRF sub-penny signing, RLP flags) so the result is triangulated. The pre-2013 odd-lot absence, the half-penny tick regime change, and the later SEC tiered round-lot redefinition are all explicitly named and gated, not buried in pitfalls. The meme-stock window (2021) is noted but not solved; running 36 months ending before the half-penny date (2011–2013 window implied) dodges the meme-stock problem but sacrifices recency.

Minor issues with Plan B: The methodology is sound and thorough, but it answers the wrong question for this firm. Even if RLOIB has a t-stat of 3.2 after costs, the IC still does not know what share of the signal is retail vs. what share is algo slicing or other institutional order batching. The effect could be real, tradeable, and still not about retail at all. Plan B then has created a signal that the firm could run, but for reasons it does not understand — a dangerous place for a concentrated manager. The earn gates (t>3.0 on net alpha) and cost breakeven framework are all sound, but they are optimizing a signal the firm should not build in the first place if the identification is bad.
issues_with_winner: Latent-class estimation (Hui-Walter) requires statistical sophistication that may not be present in-house and is not easily auditable by an investment committee without external help.

Running 36 months ending before the half-penny compliance date (inferred as 2011–2013) sacrifices 10+ years of more recent data and sidesteps rather than tests robustness to modern regime (if round lots have moved to 200+ in recent years, the old sample may not apply).

Mechanism tests on price elasticity and notional clustering are elegant but not essential; if G1–G5 pass, moving to Phase 2 does not hang on these extras, and the plan could cut them if time is short.
issues_with_loser: Starts with signal-building before establishing the core claim (round lots identify retail); if the claim is false, the entire pipeline is built on sand and the firm has sunk a month of analyst time on an unusable signal.

Does not separate the identification problem (are round lots retail?) from the trading problem (does retail flow predict returns?); if the answer to the first is 'no' or 'only partially,' the second is unanswerable from this data and the firm should have killed the project earlier.

Assumes round-lot imbalance is a meaningful retail identifier and residualizes to isolate it, rather than testing whether residualization against better retail markers (RETOIB, RLP flags) leaves any explanatory power; this is backward from the true hypothesis test.

Proposes a long-short trading framework (decile fades, short leg, beta-neutral) that does not fit the firm's actual playbook (25–30 long-hold concentrated positions over 3–5 years); even if the Sharpe is real, the firm cannot or would not run it.

Quoted capacity ('across $50M–$5B AUM') and after-cost Sharpe are invented economics; no P&L or sizing is defensible until the identification is proven and the firm has verified the effect is real and not crowded.

result.key_differentiator: Plan A builds a single-name model that cannot answer the market's actual question (does shortage-era LTA durability exist as a broad phenomenon?), while Plan B tests the mechanism itself across episodes where the outcome is already known, which is the only way to calibrate when and why agreements hold.
result.rationale:
The research question is structural: does shortage guidance portend durable revenue, and does the market already price it? This is a mechanism-test question, not a single-name KPI question. Plan A treats it as the latter.

Plan A's fatal misalignment: It builds a 'quarterly forward revenue bridge' scoring agreements by 'strength of claim' against this single company's guidance cycle, then asks whether current EV prices the modeled durable horizon correctly. This is model-then-check. But the core claim — that shortage-era LTAs survive normalized supply — is not about this company's LTA quality. It is about how all shortage-era LTAs behave. Plan A assumes the mechanism (lock-in works, durability follows from good agreement structure) and then measures whether this instance exhibits it. That is backwards. If the mechanism is false — if shortage-era LTAs are reliably repriced regardless of take-or-pay language — then Plan A's scorecard is measuring noise. If it is true, Plan A has still not proven it. The plan buries its own falsifier: reading transcripts for term drift, checking whether negative implied bookings appear, whether finished-goods inventory rises. Those are the real tests. But they happen *late*, after months building the bridge. Plan A could easily generate false conviction by finding this company looks 'good' on its scorecard, when the scorecard itself is unvalidated.

Plan B reverses this: it first establishes what actually happens when shortage LTAs normalize (using twenty to thirty historical episodes where the outcome is already observed), then applies that framework to this company. Polysilicon takes ten years to denorm fully; semiconductors reprice within two years; MLCC reprice in months. The mechanism is 'switching cost and requalification lag drive durability, not contract language.' That is falsifiable and testable. Plan B pre-registers holdouts (aerospace forgings, telecom power semis, HBM) where requalification is genuinely hard, predicting they hold. It tests that prediction on the 2021-2024 auto-semi cycle, kept blind until the framework is built. That is real validation.

For a systematic firm, Plan B is also the correct asymmetry. This is a broad-effect question: does the market overprice shortage-era LTA durability, and is that overprice tradeable across names? Type II error (missing that agreements do hold durability) has unbounded upside — capacity in many names, positive carry, crowded unwinding eventually rewards the early hold. Type I error (believing agreements hold when they reprice) is concentrated: the firm gets caught short on a repricing event with no diversification escape. Plan B's method (comparative base rates, structural qualification lags, customer-breach arithmetic) is built for Type II dominance — it asks 'where does the mechanism definitely not apply' (containers, polysilicon, MLCC) and validates on those first. Plan A's method (building a detailed scorecard for this company, checking pitfalls after the fact) is built for Type I control — but that is the wrong error to control.

Sequencing also breaks Plan A. The plan lists its own kill criteria in pitfalls (negative implied bookings, inventory divergence, definition changes) but schedules them as end-stage coherence checks, after weeks of agreement work. Kill-criteria belong first. Plan B puts them early and conditionally: does HBM hit the pre-registered checks within 12 months? If contract liabilities don't rise, or shipments don't increase, the hypothesis is falsified and the analysis stops.

Plan A is also importing the wrong economics. It calculates an 'EV/haircut-adjusted committed gross profit' and compares to peers, asking whether the market-implied durable horizon is shorter than the modeled one. But it does not answer what happens when normalized supply arrives. It models the agreement as a Tier 1/2/3 asset, but provides no historical calibration of what Tier 2 agreements (binding minimums, no cash) actually do in a repricing environment. It cites '2021-23 semiconductors' for haircut calibration, but auto-semis did *not* hold near-term durability on reprice — that is Plan B's discovery, not Plan A's input. Plan A is using Plan B's output without knowing it, and without testing whether it actually applies here.

Plan A will likely produce a detailed, confident scorecard. This company's RPO is probably well-disclosed, agreement counts can be hand-searched, and maybe the Tier 1 coverage is >60%. The analyst will report back that the analysis is 'constructive.' And the firm will price it in. But they will have no way to know whether Tier 2 agreements (the bulk of the value) actually hold, because that question was deferred to 'coherence checks' and no historical base rate was ever established. Plan B would discover that requalification on those products is cheap, prepayments are being spent on capacity expansion, and the agreements will reprice. That is the edge.

One downside to Plan B: it is cross-sectional and historical, so it cannot give this analyst a 'yes' on this company quickly. But the research question does not ask for quick. It asks whether shortage guidance portends durable revenue. That is either true or false as a mechanism, and the only way to know is to look at cases where supply normalized. Plan B does that. Plan A does not.

Plan B is also more honest about what it does not know. It outputs 'a probability-weighted haircut, not a verdict, with a statement of what would justify the higher multiple.' That is the right framing for this firm. It permits the portfolio to apply its own discount rate and capacity model. Plan A outputs a relative-valuation call (EV should be higher/lower because durable horizon is longer/shorter than priced), which overreaches; the firm cannot trade on 'the valuation is wrong' without a realization catalyst.

Confidence is 3, not 4, because Plan B is slower and will not give quick tactical color on this specific name. A PM asking 'should we buy this stock next week' will not want to wait for Plan B's framework to mature. But that PM has misframed the question. The question asks whether shortage guidance portends durability; that is a mechanism question, and mechanism questions take time. Plan A's speed is a defect, not a virtue, if it is speed on the wrong question. Plan B might also be vulnerable to definitional drift across episodes — take-or-pay means different things in polysilicon vs. semis vs. LNG. Plan B acknowledges this; Plan A does not. If Plan B's episodes are too heterogeneous to yield a clean pattern, the framework falls apart. But the plan pre-registers holdouts and hides the auto-semi holdout, which mitigates that risk. On balance, Plan B answers the question being asked, using the right error-control, with real validation. Plan A answers a different question faster.
